speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Mr. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO RAMIFICATIONS IN CANADA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Justice. Can the minister give any report to the house in connection with the investigation into the connections or ramifications disclosed by the Soble spy ring in the United States? What is the present position in Canada as to any connection between the operations of the Sobles in Canada with those carried on in the United States?

speakeroldname: Hon. Stuart S. Garson (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO RAMIFICATIONS IN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I understood that in my absence some interest was taken in this matter and in anticipation of a question such as that asked by the Leader of the Opposition I have prepared the following statements:
Hon. members will have read in the newspapers that the United States federal bureau of investigation has recently made several arrests charging residents of the United States with espionage. Under arrest are Jack and Myra Soble and Jacob Albam. As the members are aware, the policy of the Department of Justice is carefully to refrain from disclosing information relating to security matters, and the department is especially careful in this regard when the security matter concerned involves the security services of friendly nations with which we co-operate in security work. The federal bureau of investigation of the United States is one of such security services and naturally we have been co-operating with it in this case in question by investigating Canadian aspects of the case.
For obvious reasons it is quite impossible for me to disclose any facts revealed by our investigation, since these may relate to the security both of Canada and the United States; and, in addition, the members no doubt have noted that this case is sub judice in the United States courts at the present time.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO RAMIFICATIONS IN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, could the minister go so far as to say whether or not any investigation that has taken place-as revealed in the United States press-in which 82715-47i
the Royal Canadian Mounted Police were cooperating with the federal bureau of investigation indicates that any of the activities of the Sobles in connection with their business operations in this country were found to emanate from or to be connected with the U.S.S.R. or its embassy here?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO RAMIFICATIONS IN CANADA
speechtext: Well, Mr. Speaker, in line with, the position that we have always taken, I am sure my hon. friend upon reflection will consider that the question he has just asked seeks to elicit information of precisely the kind* that we avoid giving. In other words,, the information which he seeks if given might, conceivably be of more value to those who are not friendly with us than any possible value it could have in satisfying my hon. friend's curiosity.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO RAMIFICATIONS IN CANADA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would be the last to want to prejudice in any way the investigation but the information is available in the United States press and I am wondering why parliament should be denied information as to whether or not the U.S.S.R. embassy is involved in this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO RAMIFICATIONS IN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canada in common with other free countries of the world pursues the same policy, I believe, with regard to the maintaining of secrecy in relation to security matters.
Now, as my hon. friend correctly points out, when prosecutions take place in a free country the trial has to be in public, and in due course, in order to meet the necessities of these prosecutions, information has to be made public which up until that time has been kept secret. I am sure my hon. friend will agree that until the time comes when it is necessary to disclose it for the purpose of a public prosecution it is very much in the interests of ourselves and our allies that security should be maintained in relation to it.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY MR. DULLES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Prime Minister. He will have read in the press over the week end the reports of the statement made by Mr. Dulles before a Senate committee in Washington to this effect:
If I were an American boy, as you call it, going to fight in the Middle East, I would rather not have a French and British soldier, one at my left hand and one at my right. I think I would feel a lot safer.
Is there not some protest the Canadian government could make to Washington which would have the effect of stopping these provocative statements?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY MR. DULLES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman knows as all hon. members of the house know that this statement attributed to Mr. Dulles taken out of its context has been interpreted as reflecting upon the valour of French and British soldiers, and he knows that there have been given complete explanations to the effect that nothing of the kind was intended and all that was intended was to imply that, because of the feelings in the Middle East toward the British and the French arising out of the crisis connected with the Suez incident, their presence with United States troops might be more provocative than the presence of United States troops alone. I think that an expression like that taken out of its context is subject to misinterpretation. I think it is fortunate that there have been serious attempts made to clear up the misinterpretations placed upon those words.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY MR. DULLES
speechtext: Does the Prime Minister not realize that this statement has already caused grave concern in Great Britain and in France? Surely Canada, trying to get these nations together again, could help by making some protest to Washington against any such further statements being made.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY MR. DULLES
speechtext:
I do not
agree that a diplomatic protest by Canada to Washington would have the effect desired by my hon. friend.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether the Canadian government has expressed any view or indicated any policy with respect to the Kashmir situation and the action of the government of India. Have there been any discussions with other commonwealth countries as a result of this situation?
Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime
Minister): Mr. Speaker, I understand that there have been discussions as late as yesterday between the under-secretary of state for external affairs and the high commissioner of the United Kingdom, and I know there have been other discussions. I am sure the hon. gentleman appreciates, as we do, the importance of this matter and shares the hope that there will be a solution found that will not cause any serious disturbance in the relations between the various members of the commonwealth. Of course the hon. gentleman would, I am sure, agree that it is a matter about which it is difficult for other members of the commonwealth to do more than express their keen desire to be as helpful as possible to the parties in reaching an amicable settlement and that they all deplore the state of affairs that has gone on since 1947 in connection with this area of what was previously known as India.

Then are we to understand that these discussions are continuing and that the matter is still the subject of negotiation, in which case I would imagine that most hon. members might feel we should not ask for a report until the negotiations are concluded; or is it just a matter of representations having been made and the matter resting there, in which case I think we would be entitled to press to know what the representations were?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should not like to use the word "negotiations" because these discussions have been matters of consultation between the members of the commonwealth other than India and

Pakistan as to what each or all of them could do to help in bringing about an amicable settlement of the issue. From that I would not want hon. members of the house to take it that there have been no discussions of it with the representatives of both India and Pakistan. I can assure the hon. gentleman that it has been the subject of very earnest conversations along the lines, of course, that it was a matter that had to be primarily settled by those two governments but that its settlement was of great interest to all the members of the commonwealth.

Mr. John Pallet! (Peel): Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Prime Minister supplementary to that addressed to him by the hon. member for Kamloops. Would the Prime Minister advise the house whether or not the Kashmir situation was the subject of discussions between the Prime Minister and Prime Minister Nehru when he was in this country? If so, would he tell us what was that discussion and advise us if any correspondence has been exchanged between him and Prime Minister Nehru since the recent taking over by India of Kashmir?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there has been no correspondence exchanged on the subject of Kashmir with the Prime Minister of India since his visit to Ottawa. As to my confidential conversations with him, I do not think it would be proper for me to attempt to disclose them here in the house.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to address a question to the Minister of Justice. Has the minister's attention been drawn to the question asked last Wednesday regarding the Combines Investigation Act, in connection with the recent increase in the price of gasoline?

subtopic: FAUTEUX COMMISSION REPORT-ACTION TO BE TAKEN IN IMPLEMENTATION

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: FAUTEUX COMMISSION REPORT-ACTION TO BE TAKEN IN IMPLEMENTATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to ask a question of the Minister of Justice, one which I have been pursuing now for a couple of years, on probation. The minister has encouraged me to wait for the report of the Fauteux commission. This report has now been produced, and my question is whether the government has reached any decision with regard to carrying out the recommendations of this commission for action at the dominion' level.

speakeroldname: Hon. Stuart S. Garson (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FAUTEUX COMMISSION REPORT-ACTION TO BE TAKEN IN IMPLEMENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since the hon. member has been good enough to give my secretary oral notice of the question he has asked today, I have been able to prepare in reply a statement which I now present.
On July 20 last, shortly after the Fauteux report was made public, I wrote to the provincial attorneys general pointing out that the Fauteux recommendations would require for their implementation action by the parliament of Canada and the provincial legislatures of Canada; and that I therefore thought that the federal and provincial ministers should consider the report in a joint conference to this end.
In their replies to this letter the provincial authorities indicated dates for such a meeting that varied from early in the month of October to as late as mid-January of this year.
Meanwhile, we had been getting ready for such a conference and, in this connection, gathering together all the available, relevant data. This proved to be a bigger task than we had anticipated, so on October 18 I wrote to the provincial ministers to suggest that the best way of arriving at an accurate set of comparable figures for both federal and provincial ministers would be to have a meeting in Ottawa of senior federal and provincial officials for the exchange of the necessary statistical information. A meeting of senior

Inquiries of the Ministry federal and provincial officials was accordingly held in Ottawa on November 14 and 15 last, attended by representatives of all of the provinces except two.
The proceedings of this conference have been transcribed by the reporter who was in attendance. It was agreed by the meeting that the provinces would supply us with 100 copies of the statistical information which they had sent to this conference in order that we might redistribute this among the other provinces concerned.
I may say, Mr. Speaker, that we received the last of this material from the last province to report within the past 48 hours and these copies are now on their way to the provinces concerned.
The deliberations of the federal and provincial senior officials have made it clear that a large amount of work is still required to be done before either the provincial or federal governments can be in a position to discuss in any adequate manner the policy decisions that would be involved in considering the implementation of the Fauteux report.
Forthwith, after the conference at Ottawa in November last with the federal and provincial officials, the officers of the Department of Justice began work on the preparation of proposals covering the entire field of corrections which will be submitted for approval to the federal cabinet and then to a conference of federal and provincial ministers for consideration. I have already pointed out to the provincial ministers that it is difficult to predict at this time how long it will take for the proposals of the government of Canada to be placed in final form for their consideration, but that in view of the fact that we do not as yet have all of the provincial material before us-we have not had any reply from two of the provinces- and considering the multiplicity and magnitude of the problems involved, I did not see at that time how this could be done in less than five to six months.
I have informed the provincial ministers that as soon as our work is completed it is my hope that we would be able to send our proposals by mail to the provincial governments and that after they had had an opportunity to consider them, I will ask the provincial ministers concerned to meet with us in Ottawa, at a mutually acceptable time, for a discussion of the issues involved.

We were all agreed that this was the proper procedure to follow, and they on their side and we on our side are going forward with the matter as quickly as circumstances will permit.

speechtext: The minister has not answered my question.

Mr. Speaker, on Wednesday last on the orders of the day the hon. member for Hamilton South (Mr. Reinke) asked if I could comment on the question whether there are any steps which the federal government might be able to take to ensure a more rigid enforcement by the provincial governments of the Criminal Code, in view of certain representations that the hon. member stated he had received from the parents' action league in Hamilton and also in view of what he referred to as recent tragedies.
I should say at the outset that I am not aware of any failure on the part of any provincial government to enforce the Criminal Code. Be that as it may, under our system of law it is the responsibility of this parliament to enact the criminal law and it is the responsibility of the provincial governments to see to the due enforcement of that law. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Wednesday the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Hark-ness) asked if I would inform the house as to the present location of Canadian troops serving with the United Nations emergency force in the Middle East and report on their present activities. There are at present approximately 1,100 Canadian service personnel in Italy and the Middle East. Of the approximately 800 Canadian army personnel in the Middle East, roughly 600 are stationed at the United Nations emergency force base at Abu Suweir in Egypt, and approximately 200 at the United Nations emergency force headquarters at El Ballah, 30 miles south of Port Said on the Suez canal.
In accordance with the request of the United Nations our soldiers are providing communications, engineering and administrative support to the whole emergency force. The activities of these troops are, I think, sufficiently indicated by the names of the units into which they are organized. These are the Canadian

base unit, Middle East, comprising some 252 personnel; a signal squadron, composed of 182 personnel; a transport company with 208 personnel, and an infantry workshop consisting of 149 R.C.E.M.E. personnel.
I might mention that the base unit contains an engineering detachment which has been engaged in clearing mine fields, repairing roads and bridges, etc.; a detachment of medical personnel who operate a small hospital, and an ordnance detachment which handles and accounts for stores for the whole United Nations emergency force, and small detachments of other services.
The Royal Canadian Air Force now has four Otter aircraft and one Dakota stationed at Abu Suweir at the disposal of the United Nations commander, and four C-119's based at Capodichino in Italy.
The number of air force personnel presently in Italy and Egypt varies from day to day, but runs to about 220 in Italy and 80 in Abu Suweir in Egypt. It might interest hon. members to know that since the establishment of No. 435 squadron at Capodichino on November 25, 1956, a total of 106 trips has been made to Abu Suweir, and 2,932 personnel and 764,722 pounds of freight have been carried without incident or accident.
Since the departure of H.M.C.S. Magnificent, no naval personnel are now in the area.

maintopic: STATEMENT ON SELECTION OF NEW ARMOURED REGIMENT
speechtext:
While I am on my feet, Mr. Speaker, perhaps I might make a short statement in relation to the armoured regiment which is being made part of the regular army. On Friday last, I think, I stated in the house that I would be able to make an announcement shortly in that regard.
I may say that the selection of this regiment has not been an easy task, because there are a large number of armoured units in the Canadian militia which have long and distinguished histories.
The matter of seniority in the militia list, the geographical location of the unit, the intended location of the new regular unit, the location of the two existing regular armoured units, the areas of Canada now represented by units in the Canadian regular army, and a suitable national name were all factors that had to be considered.
After giving careful thought to all these factors, the decision has been taken to select the 8th Princess Louise's (New Brunswick) Hussars.
As it is considered essential that any unit selected should have a name indicating that it is a unit of the Canadian army, preferably without other local or provincial geographical connotation, the 8th Princess Louise's (New Brunswick) Hussars has been redesignated as the 8th Canadian Hussars (Princess Louise's), and the regiment, under this name, will be brought into the regular army. The regular unit will be known as the First 8th Canadian Hussars (Princess Louise's) and the militia unit will be known as the 2/8th.
The new armoured regiment will be located at Camp Gagetown, with one squadron at Valcartier, Quebec.

Mr. Chairman, this vote represents a recommendation by the government that the grants that have been made since 1951 to aid universities in the discharge of their increasing responsibilities to the Canadian public be increased, in fact, be doubled and be calculated on the basis of $1 per capita of the Canadian population instead of 50 cents per capita of the Canadian population, as has been the case heretofore. Hon. members will remember that when the Massey commission held its hearings throughout the country all Canadian universities asked for special financial assistance from the federal government and that several organizations supported that claim. The Massey commission itself felt

that such assistance was not only needed but urgent, and recommended:
That . . . the federal government make annual contributions to support the work of the universities on the basis of the population of each of the provinces of Canada.
The commission further recommended:
That these contributions be made after consultation with the government and the universities of each province, to be distributed to each university proportionately to the student enrolment.
The basis used by the commission as an illustration to determine the level of these contributions was 50 cents per head of population. It will be remembered that in 1951, after further representations from the Canadian universities and consultations with provincial governments, it was decided to recommend to parliament that that recommendation of the Massey commission be implemented. I am under the impression that it was the kind of recommendation that commended itself to practically all hon. members of the house, and an amount calculated on the basis of 50 cents per head of population has been included in the estimates ever since.
These payments were distributed directly to the institutions recognized by the provincial authorities as of university level in each province. The total amount was divided in proportion to the whole population of each province and within the province was divided among the institutions in proportion to the student enrolment in the courses leading to university degrees.
In the province of Quebec the authorities saw fit to allow this aid to be accepted for the first year only because it was stated that they feared that this was a first step towards encroachment on the exclusive jurisdiction of provincial legislatures in the field of education. I am sorry that that position was taken because I think that the institutions in Quebec could have made as good use of their share of this grant in past years as we know was made by the institutions of university level in the other provinces of Canada. I am sure that the work of the universities has been materially assisted by these grants and I do not think that their freedom and independence have been jeopardized in any way by the acceptance and use of the grants thus provided out of the appropriations made by the parliament of Canada.
In the meantime the situation of our universities has probably worsened. The most tragic aspect of this situation is undoubtedly the economic insecurity of the teaching profession. In its preliminary report the Gordon commission has stated the problem as follows:
University salaries have barely kept pace with the changes which have occurred in the price level since pre-war days. Living standards of university

teachers, especially of those in the higher ranks, have not increased with the general prosperity of the country as a whole. In fact, they have declined, and declined substantially, in relative terms.
Then a little further on:
These salaries do not bear comparison with the scales of remuneration which able men can command in business or in the professions or even with the earnings of some skilled workmen.
They go on to say:
The total annual cost of all salaries paid to assistant, associate and full professors in Canada at the present time, including deans and heads of departments, is about $12 million. As already stated we believe that it is important that the salaries of university teachers be increased very considerably.
Recently the executive council of the Canadian association of university teachers adopted unanimously a national salary scale of $8,000, $11,000 and $14,000 for assistant, associate and full professors. This scale is intended to secure to university teachers today their pre-war status and is based on 1938 average salaries multiplied by 3.5 which represents the composite increase in the cost of living and in the average real product of the Canadian worker since 1938.
The application of that new scale of salaries will involve the doubling of present salaries in central and western Canada and would require an additional annual expenditure by universities of approximately $12 million. Moreover, university enrolments are now rapidly increasing and it is expected that they will double by about 1965 which means, according to reliable estimates, that the staff of the universities should also be twice as large as it is now if young Canadians are to receive proper attention from the teaching staffs of the universities. This means that to meet our needs in this field our universities will have to devote about four times as much money on the salaries of teachers as they spend now.
We are now facing a dilemma which may be defined in simple terms. If the universities cannot spend more than at present on salaries, they will not only be unable to attract more teachers but they will be apt to lose more of the good ones they now have as, unfortunately, has been going on for some time past. In view of our rapidly increasing needs, I think this would have a pretty tragic effect on the development of Canada as a nation and I feel that all Canadians would not want such a crisis to take place. On the other hand, if universities are to fulfil their important role they must attract an increasing number of competent teachers and to do this they must be able to spend much more on salaries by 1965 than they spend at the present time.

The Gordon commission concludes its appraisal of this problem as follows:
In this connection it must suffice for us to express the strong opinion that no government which bears any share of responsibility for the future economic development of this country can allow a solution to the pressing financial problems of the universities to go by default.
That is pretty strong language but I think it is language that is fully justified by the situation facing us. According to the provisions of our constitution, it is clear that provincial governments have the main responsibilities in this field, and I think we are all confident that they will continue to meet that challenge and devote an increasing share of their rising revenues to assist Canadian universities in fulfilling their very necessary and important tasks. However, this has not been regarded in the past as their exclusive responsibility and I hope it will not be regarded in the future as their exclusive responsibility. Private foundations in industry, both in Canada and from abroad, have made important contributions in the past to help our universities arid the teachers in them. While we hope that private contribution's from other countries, especially those with which we have the closest relations, will be continued,-perhaps even that they might be increased-I am sure that hon. members have noted with great satisfaction the active interest which Canadian industry has shown more recently in this field. Our business men realize more and more that they can no longer afford to be indifferent to the financial problems of our universities, and they have initiated projects which, if fully implemented, will have most beneficial effects. These developments will be most reassuring for all of us-and I am sure that is the overwhelming majority -who want to see not only the survival but the expansion of private institutions of higher learning in Canada and who believe that the diversification of sources of revenue is the best method by which our universities can achieve and maintain the highest degree of intellectual freedom and intellectual independence.
While there is general agreement that provincial governments and private industry should increase their assistance to universities, there are Canadians who feel that the Canadian government should not intervene in this field. I cannot share that view. I believe that the Canadian government has the constitutional right to offer assistance to universities and that it is its duty and responsibility to do so. After all the Canadian people through their elected representatives are the greatest consumer in numbers of the training that is given to our young people in

Supply-Finance
our Canadian universities. If we did not have the Canadian universities to give them that training, we might be in the same position as that in which we find ourselves with respect to the training of officers and directors of our armed forces and be obliged to establish, maintain and operate special schools for their training. I think that would be a great misfortune. I think it would be a great misfortune if the civil servants in the ordinary administration of their fellow citizens' affairs were not trained in the same way and were not regarded as part of the general public about whose affairs they are obliged to busy themselves.
I have seen countries where there seemed to be one group that was the government group, going from the prime minister right down through every degree of civil servant, whilst the governed were another group. That is not the way in which we have been brought up. That is not our way of life. In our democratic institutions it is the people themselves who select from among themselves, directly or through their representatives, those who are entrusted with the administration of such of their affairs as must be administered for the group at large. I think that is a more healthy situation than would be the case if we trained a certain number of young Canadian citizens for the occupancy of any ivory towers of civil administration.
It is on the same general basis of its constitutional right to devote funds from the consolidated revenue fund to national needs that the federal government has distributed, through the national research council, an amount of approximately $25 million since 1917 for postgraduate research in the field of the national sciences, these amounts being distributed to individuals and to universities. A great number of other federal programs have the same constitutional basis. Family allowances; the national health program; our financial contributions to pensions for the blind and for disabled persons; our assistance to technical and vocational training and to the unemployed; our equalization payments to the provinces; our contributions under the Canada Forestry Act and the Canada Water Conservation Assistance Act, as well as others, belong to the same category of services which are primarily a provincial responsibility but which are of national concern and have benefited from the appropriations by this parliament to assist in carrying them out. All these programs have common features. They are financed through the consolidated revenue fund. They do not involve any element of compulsion and they

apply to classes of responsibilities which relate to matters within the legislative jurisdiction of the provinces but they do not amount to legislation controlling the administration or the operations of these functions.
From the origin of confederation provincial governments have accepted most of these programs and have participated in the financing of some of them without questioning their constitutional validity. They themselves have used the same continuation of the royal prerogative to apply public funds to matters that would be of value to the national development or to the welfare of the nation as a whole. In my own province where there have been these fears expressed about the constitutional right to make these grants the government, with the authority of the legislature itself, has made similar grants to educational institutions outside the limits of the province. I think the first was made for the University of Ottawa many many years ago, and they have continued to be made. I think they have helped to develop this feeling of interdependence of the people of one area and the people of another area. We feel-and I think parliament has accepted that provision-that it was proper to make grants in aid to further the good work of the universities. Of course, no one is obliged to accept these grants. But their acceptance has not in the past led to any undermining of the legislative jurisdiction of the provincial legislatures in respect of such activities, and I do not think it will do so in the future.
Federal assistance to the universities also raises the question of policy. I think that policy has been, six times already, decided by this house in respect of the earlier grants. I hope an increase, which will amount to approximately one dollar per head in all of the Canadian population, will be regarded as a proper contribution to make to their work.
In order to try to make it appear more obvious that there was no attempt whatsoever to control the activities of or to legislate with respect to the operations of the universities we are making the following recommendation instead of making direct payments to the individual institutions. We are not concerned with the individual institutions as individual institutions. We are concerned nationally with the effect of the university services to the Canadian nation. We are now recommending that instead of having cheques written out by the Department of Finance to each individual institution, the total amount appropriated by parliament for aid to the universities will be turned over to the National Council of Canadian Universities which has been incorporated recently and which, through

its appointees, has agreed that it would accept the duty of receiving this amount en bloc from the federal treasury and of apportioning it on the basis as between provinces of the population of each province and on the basis within the province of the number of student enrolments in each institution recognized as being of university level in that province.
Hon. members will have noted that the item in the estimates provides that the amount which had been previously voted in the general estimates under vote 132 of the Appropriation Act No. 6, 1956, will be applied in the same way. In the past these votes, though made during the winter season, were not paid to the universities until late January or in the course of the month of February of the next calendar year. It was felt that if parliament were to consider that it was proper to increase the amount of the aid to the universities to an amount equal to $1 per capita of the Canadian population in view of the existing circumstances, it would not be proper to wait to give effect to that decision until the month of February, 1958. For that reason, this additional amount which will bring the vote up to practically $16 million is set out in language which will make it the duty of the Minister of Finance, after entering into a contract with the incorporated body, the National Council of Canadian Universities, to pay the whole amount over almost at once, as soon as the legislation becomes effective, so that it will be available for use in this calendar year and will not be retarded until the calendar year 1958.
I have been asked why there was this system of turning the grant over to the National Council of Canadian Universities instead of continuing to make the payments to each insitution individually. Well, I had hoped, and I still hope, that ultimately it will convince the people who require university services throughout the whole of Canada that there is no intention and no possibility of this impinging upon the exclusive legislative jurisdiction of the respective provinces; that it is something which the Canadian government feels, in the interests of the Canadian people represented by the Canadian government, ought to be done in order to compensate for the direct value it receives from those university services in the training of the personnel fitted to occupy the offices in the administration which as the population increases and as the economy becomes more productive, are increasing in responsibilities and do require trained minds properly to administer the legislation which the representatives of the people adopt in their parliament.
So that there may be no suggestion that the whole Canadian people are being taxed for

the benefit of only a portion or only certain regions of the country we want to provide that these amounts, if they are not taken immediately, will remain as a trust in the hands of the National Council of Canadian Universities to be applied for whenever the institution to which they would have been allocated sees fit to apply for them or until parliament sees fit to dispose of them otherwise. These are the terms that are set out in this vote.
Hon. members will recall that in the other votes it was the Minister of Finance who was to determine by regulations the various details that would go to fix what would be the meaning of university level and such other details. Well, all this will be set out in the contract entered into between the government and the National Council of Canadian Universities. As soon as that contract is entered into it will be tabled here and hon. members will see that the draft that is being discussed makes no change in the manner in which the calculations were to be made for the appropriate allocation as between provinces and as between institutions within the provinces in the previous votes for the lesser amounts.
I trust that any misgivings which may exist anywhere as to the possibility of the Canadian parliament wishing to trespass on the jurisdiction of the provincial legislatures in respect of education will disappear and that it will be recognized that this is something that is in the interests of the nation as a whole, that is almost indispensable to the proper development of the nation as a whole, and that it will not in any way lessen the feeling of responsibility of the provincial governments or of those other employers of trained minds whether they be industrial or commercial firms or be other like organizations which are beginning to recognize-and I trust they will continue in their recognition -their responsibility-to do their share so that we may continue to have-I think we have had it in the past-university service of which we shall have every reason to be satisfied and be proud; that we shall continue to have the kind of university services that are necessary for the proper development of a nation that has tremendous natural resources, that has been very benevolently blessed by Providence in the area and richness of its land, and which I feel is to be the earthly home of an increasing number of reasonable-minded, well-trained members of the human family who will not only provide good living conditions for themselves in their own land but will continue to make their contribution to the welfare and improvement of human life throughout

Supply-Finance
as large an area of the terrestrial globe as their influence may happen to reach.

Mr. Chairman, the Prime Minister has been at pains to give us a very full and clear exposition of the reasons underlying the grants to universities and the change in the routing of the money, so to speak. I think there will be the widest measure of agreement in this house as to the desirability of assisting universities. That was covered in considerable detail the other day and I shall pause only for a moment or two to comment on what the Prime Minister said about the teaching profession. I think we will all agree with that.
I suppose it may be said that the manner in which those in the teaching profession are treated in a country is a sign of the degree of its civilization and I have sometimes been worried that in our own country we do not treat those in the teaching profession as we should, and this is particularly true in times of great prosperity. It was true in the gay twenties, in the thirties things levelled up better, and now again there has been a falling behind.
It is not disagreeing in the least with what the Prime Minister said concerning what is needed to be done if one offers one or two comments about the teaching profession. There are, of course, those dedicated spirits who regard the teaching profession as a way of life and who would be in it even if it involved something approaching starvation. I remember a professor of mine who sought my assistance one day in the preparation of his income tax. This was a good many years ago and at that time he was earning the munificent salary of $6,000 a year which he thought was a very good salary. I said that I did not agree with him and that he ought to receive the same amount of remuneration as a successful businessman. "Oh," he said, "but look at the kind of work I am doing. Why, if I were a man of means I would be ready to put down a premium to be allowed to do it". Well, Mr. Chairman, there are not many people like that, although there are some and in varying degrees there are dedicated spirits who would teach even though they had to suffer in order to do so. Also as a way of life we must not forget it has great attractions. It offers leisure which the rest of us do not enjoy and I say that not in order to disagree with what has been put forward as to the need but merely to draw attention to these aspects.
We come now to the actual grants. The Prime Minister has explained in considerable detail the reasons for the new method of routing the money. The Prime Minister

very naturally is interested in the constitutional aspect of it which is seriously regarded in certain quarters and he has been at pains to explain it to us. Then we come to the national conference of Canadian universities. I suppose it would be a fairly accurate description of the use of the conference if I said it is to be used rather like a conduit pipe for the transfer of the money from the government to the universities. Well, a conduit pipe has not a very elevated function but it is useful and therefore I do not see that it is of vital importance whether the national conference of Canadian universities or the present system is used. I somewhat regret that the national conference will be used because it does not seem to me to be a natural function for it. I do not believe it is incorporated although it will become incorporated.
The letters patent under part 2, I think it is, of the Companies Act were issued on January 18.

Thank you. The Prime Minister has I think covered one point which is necessary to be covered. I think it is clear from what he said that the national conference is not to have any discretion whatsoever in the matter of apportioning the funds. I think it would be not only unfortunate but most undesirable if any discretion were left, and that leads me to express the hope that the Prime Minister will give us some indication of the agreement which is to be entered into and which I assume will give definite directions to the national conference as to how the money is to be paid.
I have already said I rather regret that this method is to be used. In the first place it seems to me it is introducing a piece of machinery which we could very well have done without. Nevertheless I do not think it is a matter one should take too seriously and on the understanding which I got from the Prime Minister's speech that there will be no discretion left to the conference and that it will merely pass this money on, then it seems to me we come to the question as to whether or not we are prepared to increase the grants to the universities from 50 cents per head of population to $1; in other words, to double the grants. As I understand it, these grants go to the universities free of strings of any kind and I can speak for one university which has received its grant with very great thankfulness.
I do not think there is anything I need to add. Other grants for universities with a view to capital expenditures will be discussed and that need not be gone into now.

As I said, Mr. Chairman, I am not following the Prime Minister in discussing the constitutional details of the situation because that is a matter that concerns him and the government, and I can understand how much it does concern them; I think I shall content myself with what I have said.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, we welcome this supplementary estimate which is now before us. We welcome the decision of the government to double the amount of money to be paid by way of grants to our Canadian universities. We also welcome most heartily the speech that has been made today by the Prime Minister.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I note that it is welcomed in all quarters of the house. I merely want to say, Mr. Chairman, that it is a speech that would have been most welcome yesterday.
Hear, hear.
The Minister of Justice is not listening.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: As a matter of fact I noticed that part of the speech the Prime Minister made today was from a manuscript and I think it is unfortunate that he had not shown a copy of that manuscript to the Minister of Justice before that hon. gentleman made the speech he gave us last evening.
The Minister of Justice is looking very busy now.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, the Canadian people are going to be somewhat confused by the news that is coming out of Ottawa these days with respect to the question of education. One day the news is that the government is all for the assisting of education in this country. On another day the news is that the government is against it, that the Minister of Justice has pronounced upon the subject and has said it is contrary to the constitution. Come another day and the Prime Minister says that education is something that is in the interest of the nation as a whole and that it is almost indispensable, in the interests of the nation as a whole, that something should be done about its financial support. I know that a line is drawn by the government between university education and general education at other levels, and the Minister of Justice is slightly on one side of it and the Prime Minister is slightly on the other side. Surely any reasonable person in Canada who is interested in the welfare of this country would agree that what the Prime Minister said today about the importance of education and about the concern of the nation as a whole in education
Supply-Finance
applies to all levels of education just as much as it applies to university education. I say again that we welcome most heartily the excellent speech the Prime Minister made today. I am only sorry the Minister of Justice did not know that this speech was going to be made before he presented the remarks which he placed on the record last night.
In connection with this attempt to draw the line between university education and education generally may I remind the Minister of Justice of something with which he must be familiar, coming as he does from the same province which I have the honour to represent. He knows that in Manitoba grade 12 in high school is the equivalent of first year in our universities. As a matter of fact many of the courses taught in the first year of university, in both arts and science, are almost identical with some of the courses taught in grade 12. Boys and girls of around 17 years of age going to grade 12 in the high schools of Manitoba are in an educational system which according to the Minister of Justice cannot receive any financial assistance from the federal treasury because the constitution stands in the way, but other young men and women of the same age are going to the University of Manitoba or its affiliated colleges and taking exactly the same courses and according to the Prime Minister it is in the national interest that those institutions be assisted financially out of the federal treasury. I agree with the Prime Minister and I disagree thoroughly with the position taken yesterday by the Minister of Justice.
I hope that the growing interest in the importance of this question which was evinced by the excellent speech made today by the Prime Minister means that what we know is true will soon come to pass, that the day will come when out of the federal treasury there will be substantial grants of money for this important national interest, the interest of the education of our people.
The Prime Minister put it very well in what he said today about what education means to the community, to the government, to the civil service and to our people generally. If education means all of that to this nation and requires that the federal government find ways and means to provide financial aid at the university level, we submit that it applies to education generally. The only criticism I have to make of the Prime Minister's speech is that he did not rise in his place yesterday and make the same speech on the motion moved by my colleague, the hon. member for Saskatoon.
The Prime Minister has been confronted with the difficulty of finding some way in

Supply-Finance
which to make these grants to universities without paying them to the provincial governments or directly to the universities themselves. He has come up with this very interesting device-I have no quarrel with it at all-of paying the money to the National Conference of Canadian Universities so that that body may in turn channel it along to the universities themselves.
I was interested in the exchange which took place a moment ago between the hon. member for Greenwood and the Prime Minister. The hon. member for Greenwood thought that the National Conference of Canadian Universities was not an incorporated organization, but the Prime Minister came right back to say that letters patent had been issued recently putting that organization in the position where it could receive and handle this money. If the government is to be logical in this and recognize the importance which education generally plays in the life of this country it could probably suggest that letters patent be issued to the Canadian association of school trustees so that federal money could be made available to assist education down the line.
We welcome the education which is taking place on the other side of the house. We welcome the realization which is growing, as expressed in the Prime Minister's speech, of the importance of this question and we hope that it will not be long until we see a real extension of this principle in terms of the precepts laid down today by the Prime Minister.
I want to say just a few words with particular reference to the province from which I come. Thus far I have been speaking on behalf of our entire group in welcoming what the Prime Minister has said today, but as one coming from Manitoba I wish to point out that in our province there is a particular need for increased financial aid at the university level. All of us in Manitoba will be delighted that the amount to be made available to our institutions at the university level will be doubled as far as our province is concerned. As other hon. members from my province know, some months ago we lost from our university the entire staff of teachers in the faculty of education. Those teachers were lost to a university which was able to pay higher salaries.
They were attracted there.4 It was not a matter of salaries at all, it was the better working conditions and the fact that it is a nicer province.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
The Minister of Fisheries never misses a chance to put in a plug for the climate and some of the other advantages

of the province of British Columbia, but some of the rest of us feel that there is nothing like the invigorating effect of life on the prairies. As I was saying, a year ago we lost the teaching staff of an entire faculty because of the inability of the University of Manitoba to pay salaries equal to those that could be paid somewhere else. In recent weeks there has been great concern at the University of Manitoba with respect to another faculty, the faculty of engineering. There is grave danger that some of the professors in that faculty may leave for the very same reason, because the salary scale at the University of Manitoba is inadequate.
Strong representations have been made to the university and the provincial authorities in Manitoba by representatives of the students. I am sure all of us who recall our college and university days will be interested in reading of this delegation of students going to the university authorities. I remember some strange things we went to the authorities about in my day but I do not recall that we ever urged that the professors should receive higher pay. Such is the state of university salaries at the present time, such is the seriousness of the situation created by the possible loss of professors by certain universities that that is what students are organizing for at the present time. They are trying to persuade the authorities to pay a higher scale of salaries to the professors in the engineering and other faculties in the University of Manitoba.
I could go on and speak of other difficulties facing the University of Manitoba. A minor tragedy occurred during the early part of the winter when a chemistry laboratory was destroyed by fire. This was just an old hut in which chemistry experiments were being carried on, but its loss underlines the need, not only for paying adequate salaries to professors but for providing buildings and other capital equipment.
So I say that in Manitoba, and I know the same is true in some other provinces, the need is very great. There is a crisis at the university level just as there is a crisis in education generally, as was indicated yesterday by the hon. member for Saskatoon. We feel that very serious attention must be given to this matter.
We do not want the government to take the view that because we welcome this larger grant, that so far as we are concerned it is the end of the story. We feel that sooner or later there will have to be a real grappling by all governments in this country with this problem. They will have to sit down together and consider the whole problem of the financing of education. At its very

beginning this country made the decision that in terms of education we would be a democracy, we would make education available to everyone. I for one do not think that we made a mistake. However, if we are going to continue to adhere to the principle that education should be made available to everyone we are going to have to face these increasing costs. We are going to have to provide for them in ways that are sensible, in ways that relate to the nature of our economy at the present time. I am glad to hear the Prime Minister say that the federal government has the prerogative of making grants wherever it feels that the making of such grants is in the national interest. I am glad, too, that he underlined the right of the provincial governments to make grants wherever they feel that they are in the interests of the community generally. Nothing could be of greater interest to life in this country, and to the future of Canada, than the channelling into education of the proportion of our total national wealth that it needs and deserves. Toward that end I hope there will be further progress in the near future. Again, I say, we welcome this estimate; we shall vote for it gladly. We also welcome the speech of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). We regret he did not make it yesterday. We hope he will make it the next time the broader question of aid to education, without-in his own terms-interfering with exclusive provincial jurisdiction, comes before this house, as come it will.

Mr. Chairman, I intend to
take just a minute on this item. I appreciate the views that have just been expressed with respect to the Prime Minister's speech this afternoon, and how appropriate it would have been had he made the same speech yesterday on a previous resolution, even though that resolution was sponsored by a private member. I may say that I am alarmed, however, that the government, with its huge majority, voted against that resolution yesterday-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: They talked it out.

They talked it out, yes, but
if they had voted on it the effect would have been the same, because the Minister of Justice himself gave the lead in one of the closing speeches. I am surprised at that, because the whole tenor of the speeches made yesterday by those on the government side of the house was to the effect that they were not in favour of the motion as proposed by the hon. member for Saskatoon.
I noted, Mr. Chairman, that the Prime Minister made reference in his speech to certain regulations which must be laid down,
Supply-Finance
and in accordance with which the council of universities will administer this money. I agree that there must be some sort of regulations governing this matter; I do not know what those regulations are going to be. It occurs to me that we might have been given some elaboration of that subject; I am inclined to think that, perhaps, the small colleges may be left out in the cold.
I am a believer in the small college; I believe the small college is of great value to the general educational progress of our nation. I have been connected with small colleges during part of my life-time experience, and I believe they have a very important part to play in our national life. I am sometimes amazed at the way in which we grind out the students who go forth from our high schools and universities-it is just like grinding them out of a mill. I wonder sometimes if they do not leave our schools of higher learning as if they had been turned out by an assembly line process which results in all of them knowing and believing the same things. I wonder if there is any real individual thinking among them.
I believe that the smaller college gives more personal attention to the student, and for that reason alone such colleges are of particular value. It is one thing to educate a mind; it is another thing to educate the personality. There is a difference between loading the mind with figures and facts and teaching the mind to think for itself. I am a great believer in individual freedom, and I believe the best possible education that can be given to our young people, and the most valuable education to provide for the nation, is the production of minds trained to think for themselves. When this is the object of education you do not get the stereotyped mind; you get independent thinking-and independent thinking is that which has made history. I make a plea for the smaller colleges on that account.
I suppose, Mr. Chairman, that there are a good many small colleges which are affiliated to universities, but there may be other types of colleges which are not. Let us remember this; education does not come only through a recognized university. Some of our young people, while desiring to think properly, also desire to use their hands. I do not know whether there will be any assistance here for some of our technical colleges. Some of our young people like to go in for agriculture. I know there are agricultural subjects taught in some of our universities, but I would be interested to know whether certain of our agricultural colleges may gain assistance from these grants. Then, again,

Supply-Finance
there are religious colleges. There are a good many young people who wish to enter a school of religion, and there are some , independent colleges connected with churches of one kind or another. All these things constitute what I would call a proper educational system for the nation as a whole, yet a lot of these smaller colleges have to go begging for money. Some of them are organized on a voluntary basis; some of them have to go out and appeal for funds from their congregations or from donors who may be particularly interested in an individual organization. I wonder whether any assistance would be given to such colleges as these from the funds which will be made available.
It is no mean fund; it is $7,986,000 a year, plus what has already been appropriated.
Mr. Speaker, I do not think I wish to say anything else. We are in favour of the appropriation, but I would just voice this plea for the smaller colleges.

I want to make a few remarks on this important subject, to express, particularly, my own pleasure at the increased support to the universities which this item represents. After listening to the remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre I am inclined to suggest that in this field of support to university education we have come a great distance in a relatively short time, and I believe, personally, that the wide public support which has been given to this assistance to the universities is the result, primarily, of the sympathy with which the Prime Minister has presented this problem not only to the house but to the people of Canada.
Before coming to the house as a member I had the opportunity to teach at a university in Nova Scotia and since that time I have been rather close to the administration, and have learned the very wholesome effects which have followed from this assistance. Now the assistance is to be doubled and further beneficial effects will flow. Several years ago St. Francis Xavier University at Antigonish opened a junior college in Sydney which now gives the first year in university education, particularly to the sons of coal miners, steel workers and others in the area Who might not be able to leave their homes to go to a distant place. Just a year ago I had the opportunity of talking to the principal of Xavier junior college and he gave me a very vivid and impressive account of the good work that was being done not only in the academic field but also in other adult classes and he suggested that without the assistance provided through these university grants it would be next to impossible

for this small community college to carry on this very useful work.
I believe further that the assistance now given in Nova Scotia and the maritimes generally, despite certain improvements that some of us would like to see, has meant a great deal to the smaller colleges to which the hon. member for Macleod has made reference. Twenty years ago there was a greater crisis in education in the maritime provinces than there is today in the sense that a great discussion took place on the desirability of university centralization. The advocates of centralization were unable to achieve their objective and the result is that we have in many parts of Nova Scotia today outstanding smaller universities which are giving not only good academic courses but are providing outstanding community and cultural leadership in various parts of the province. I do know that eastern Nova Scotia would be much poorer without the existence of St. Francis Xavier and I do know that the Annapolis valley would be much poorer without the existence of Acadia university.
The system of university assistance now in vogue permits a continued decentralization policy and does not in any sense attempt to centralize or bring together the whole university community into one locality as used to be advocated. It is very interesting also to observe that the trend today, as reflected in the remarks of the hon. member for Macleod, is towards a greater emphasis on the smaller community college, and this trend has reached its greatest development in the United States. I believe that the system of making these payments adopted by the House of Commons is helpful to the small liberal arts college and university and, indeed, some of the apprehensions expressed by the hon. member for Macleod do not come about because all of the church supported universities, provided they meet the required qualifications, receive assistance. There is certainly no effort to make a choice as between church schools and secular schools.
I was particularly pleased with the emphasis that the Prime Minister placed on the salary schedules existing in Canadian universities. There is an emphasis, sometimes too great, on building programs and on the development of great physical plants. But no matter what buildings are erected on university campuses, a university is still made up of professors, books and now, in a technical era, laboratories, and no great expansion of physical plant will replace the quality of professors who are the human medium of instruction.
I know it has been very difficult for young men in this country to continue their

academic careers in the universities because of the lower salary schedules and because of the greater inducements offered by industrial and other occupations in the country. No single feature of this item appeals to me more than the capacity which it provides to Canadian universities to spend more money on the very indispensable part of a university, namely, its professors.
It is true that the assistance herein provided is not a final answer to the financing of universities. Universities will be expected to continue to cultivate their own private sources of assistance. That is all to the good because it is important that voluntary agencies and private individuals through their personal connection with the universities continue their interest in the cause of higher education.
I do not intend to go into the constitutional aspect of the problem but no matter what can be said on the constitutional phase it is still a truism that the universities are national institutions. If you consider, for example, the total number of graduates from any of the universities in Nova Scotia you will find that about 35 per cent serve in other provinces of Canada. Even if you consider the graduates of the larger universities in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec you will also find that many of these graduates do not remain in their own provinces but go and offer their services in the other provinces of Canada. Therefore there is a great and very wide circulation of graduates from provincial universities throughout the whole of Canada. These services are offered everywhere and point up very clearly that the universities of our country are national institutions and are deserving of national support.
I certainly welcome this particular item and I am sure that if this session is not notable for anything else it will be notable in the university communities of Canada for the very great strides made by parliament and the government in giving practical form to the great desire we all have to support the universities and the students of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I have been
thinking exactly as the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond has been thinking, that whatever else may be said of this session or whatever else may be said before we are through and possibly experience a more tumultuous atmosphere than has heretofore characterized this chamber, no session has ever had so much to do with education as the present one since we opened on January 8. With the cultural council, with the resolution of the hon. member for Saskatoon, with the philosophical and learned address
Supply-Finance
with which the Prime Minister opened the debate this afternoon, certainly this is a most unique session. I am sure there are those in the house, including myself in the very short time I have been here, who remember that when we started to discuss this item in 1951 we were told by some gentlemen who occupy rather prominent positions in the house: You should not urge that, do not ask for anything more, you know, it is such a risky proposition, the government is on such dangerous ground that the subject is very likely to be dropped, and please say nothing about it or else that will happen to it.
When we hear the forthright, intelligent and able presentation of the Prime Minister this afternoon with respect to this question we can realize how far the house and the government have progressed along this line in the days since the item was first introduced in 1951, I believe the Prime Minister said. Certainly we can all heartily agree with all that he said.
I am not going to take the time to discuss the matter at any length now. I have expressed my opinion on it in times gone by. I gather from the Prime Minister that we are going to operate under exactly the same formulas as have prevailed heretofore except that the amount will be $1 instead of 50 cents and the amount will be paid to the council or conference rather than paid to the universities by the Department of Finance. I am sure we all welcome very heartily the 100 per cent increase in the contribution.
I do not have to emphasize the problems of the universities today. The hon. member for Inverness-Richmond suggested that the problems were not as great as they were at one time.
That is possibly true, Mr. Chairman, though I doubt it. The one thing I would regret most in the Prime Minister's speech this afternoon was the reading of the salary scale which has now been suggested and approved for university professors across Canada. I can imagine the reactions of certain university professors. I am sure if our friend the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond were still carrying on as a professor at St. Francis Xavier and saw that salary scale, he would be discussing that night with his wife whether he should remain or whether he should seek those western fields where salary scales are much higher. I am sure the same thing would prevail in other places in Canada.
That is only an objective.

My friend from Queens University is issuing a warning to his faculty members that it is only an objective.

Supply-Finance
One thing I would say seriously in connection with this matter is this. I regret again, as I have expressed regret previously, that this system cannot be so administered as to take care of some of the inequalities which exist and which will continue to exist between universities because of the mechanical basis on which the grant is made.
We welcome the grant. I agree with the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond that it is going a substantial distance or at least some distance in meeting the problems of the universities. But those problems are increasing so rapidly, as the Prime Minister himself intimated, that I doubt if this has gone far in solving problems that were in existence even 10 or 15 years ago.
In the east, in our own maritime provinces, we have the situation of the small college to which my friend referred. I certainly cannot forgo the opportunity of returning the compliment and saying that eastern Nova Scotia and in fact all Nova Scotia and the maritimes would be much poorer if it were not for the leadership given in the past and still being given by St. Francis Xavier in the eastern part of the province. Everyone in the east and I think everyone in Canada knows of the contribution that university has made to the educational and social problems of Canada.
I must not take more time, except to say again that I welcome the making of this grant; but because of the fact that we have a large number of universities, a relatively small population and a very large student population coming from all over Canada, the same disparity will exist. I think of my own university, for instance. I am not trying to quote the figures correctly but roughly $94, I think, was received last year in our case as compared with over $200 in other institutions.
I have expressed the hope and I am confident-that is why I am happy to see it- that this is another step along the road upon which we are just now starting. That is why I welcome this step. I am confident' that sooner or later you are going to build into this machinery an equalization arrangement so there will be a minimum per student, at any rate, such as that used during the war in connection with the veterans, when I think it was $125 per student or something of the kind. If that were done it would be a big improvement. The cost to the treasury would be relatively small, and it would be of assistance to the smaller universities which do not receive provincial grants. There are no provincial universities in Nova Scotia. They are all privately financed. If an arrangement such as this were made it would go a long way toward rectifying the situation. Hence we welcome this grant. As I said, the students of

history will look back at this as the year in which the government and the parliament of Canada embarked upon the new road in so far as education is concerned.

I have three questions. The first is this. Does the one dollar per capita represent a relative amount compared to the costs of operating universities at the time the 50 cent grant was made? The second question is this. Is there any other reason why the grants are not made on a per capita basis to the provinces instead of to the national council of Canadian universities? The third question is, will these grants from the national council of Canadian universities be free of all obligations as to standards, curriculum or the hiring of the teaching personnel?
One other suggestion I should like to make is this. I wonder if it would be possible in any way to direct some of this grant to a revolving fund which would assist underprivileged students to get to university. I think a student who is worth his salt would like to pay his own way and, if it were possible for him to do so after he had taken his university training, pay back that amount of money so it would leave the way open for some underprivileged person to follow in his wake and take the university training he so greatly desires.

Mr. Chairman, like all other hon. members who have spoken on this subject, I am greatly alarmed by the difficult situation which the Canadian universities are in at the present time. Like all other hon. members in this	house I have	the	greatestrespect for my	own	alma	mater,	namelyLaval University. I can easily picture all the problems that face this great institution at the present time, having regard to the increase in the cost of living, the increase in the cost of materials, and various other difficulties which the authorities of this great university	must	face	at	the	presenttime. However,	I am	sorry	to	be the only
voice so far which has been raised against this vote.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
