speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 4, to amend the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am sure it will be unnecessary for me to speak for more than a few minutes in moving the second reading of this bill, which has been before the house every year since 1948. In most sessions it has been debated, so the arguments for and against it have been presented a number of times. It is, of course, my hope that since all political parties in this country have gone on record as favouring the principle which underlies this bill, since three of the parties in this house, together with individual members on the government side, have voted for it a number of times, one of these times the bill will pass and its principle will be written into our federal statutes.
The purpose of the bill is to incorporate what is known as the voluntary revocable check-off into the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. The voluntary revocable check-off is a provision that makes it possible for any union that has been certified according to law to request of the employer that deductions be made from the wages of the employees in the bargaining unit to apply toward their union dues. The provision is a standard one which includes the requirement that even after a certified union makes its request it shall apply only to those members of the union who personally sign such a request, with the understanding that any such member may at any time revoke that request if he wishes to do so. That is the reason for this provision being styled as the voluntary revocable check-off of trade union dues.
I would point out, Mr. Speaker, that a provision similar to this one is in the labour codes of a number of the provinces of this country and, as I have already indicated, the principle of union security, of which this is the barest minimum, has been supported at political conventions by all the major parties of this country.
The wording of my bill is taken from wording which was written into the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act when that bill was in the hands of the industrial relations committee back in 1948. I must make it clear that the provision was not in the bill when the government brought it in, but it was put in by the committee on the motion of the then member for Spadina
Industrial Relations
who is now a member of the other place. However, despite the majority vote of the industrial relations committee of that parliament for this provision, it was struck out by a majority vote of the house when the bill came back to committee of the whole. Since that time quite a number of Liberal members on occasion have spoken and voted for this provision, along with members of the three parties on this side of the house. This is what leads me to hope that one of these days parliament as a whole will recognize that this tribute to the position of organized labour in our economy should be included in our labour laws.
Not only has there been all kinds of support for this principle to which I have already referred but I would point out that in 1953 the house, while refusing to give second reading to Bill No. 2 of that year, it being identical with Bill No. 4 which is now before us, nevertheless referred its subject matter to the committee on industrial relations. I have before me the second report of the committee on industrial relations which was presented to the house on Tuesday, April 28, 1953. It is not very long. I should like, therefore, to read it to the house:
The standing committee on industrial relations begs leave to present the following as its second report.
Your committee has considered the subject matter of Bill No. 2, "An act to amend Ithe Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act (voluntary revocable check-off)", and has agreed to report as follows:
Your committee endorses the principle of Bill No. 2 and recommends that the principle of the said bill, together with the submissions included in the printed minutes of proceedings and evidence of the committee on the subject matter of this bill, be considered by the government in its review and proposed revision of the provisions of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, which the committee is informed is now under study.
A copy of the minutes of proceedings and evidence of your committee is appended.
All of which is respectfully submitted.
It is signed by the chairman of the committee of that session.
I would point out also, Mr. Speaker, that on May 5, 1953, the chairman of that committee moved in the House of Commons that the report of the committee be concurred in by the house. There was a short debate which is recorded on about a page or so of Hansard, at the end of which that motion for concurrence was adopted.
I mention the fact that there was a short debate just to make it clear that it was not one of those pro forma votes. The house, I suggest, knew what it was doing when it concurred in this report, and thus made it the view of the house as a whole that the principle of Bill No. 2 of that year was endorsed and its study recommended to the

Industrial Relations
government in its review and proposed revision of the provisions of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act.
Well, Mr. Speaker, we learned later that study, of course, was given by the government, and no doubt it is still being given, to the subject matter of the bill, the principle underlying it, but that seems to be as far as the government has gone in relation to this pretty clear-cut recommendation which was made to it by the House of Commons in 1953, just before an election, of course, with respect to a report made to the house by a committee.
I mention that, Mr. Speaker, in support of my contention that this principle of having the check-off of trade union dues is something to which a great deal of thought and study have been given, something which has wide support and something which many of us feel should be put on the statute books as a recognition of the important and rightful place the trade union movement has in the economy of our country.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, the arguments for this proposal are on the pages of Hansard of the past eight or nine years and therefore it is not necessary for me to speak at any greater length. However, I have pleasure once again in presenting to the house this bill to provide for the voluntary revocable check-off of trade union dues.

speechtext:
The government of the day had been elected, I believe, in June of that year with perhaps the largest majority that any government had ever had in the House of Commons. For that reason I found it impossible to vote for the measure at that time. As I said, it was the cause of a considerable measure of embarrassment for me, but when explained to reasonable thinking people they understood my position. I mention this simply to substantiate what the hon. member said regarding the length of time it has been before the house.
I would say this legislation would not have far-reaching consequences in this day and

age, because most locals covered by union agreements already have the check-off or a greater measure of union security. If I recall correctly the figures given by the Minister of Labour on a previous occasion, approximately 85 or 90 per cent of those who come directly under the federal Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act already have some measure of union security, either check-off, closed shop or union shop; therefore it would not have a far-reaching effect. However, the principle is one to which I personally subscribe and am certainly willing to support.
I believe it was back in 1946 that I took part in a labour lobby which appeared before the cabinet of the legislature of the province of British Columbia, and we put forth very strong arguments in favour of check-off being written into the labour act of that province. If my memory serves me correctly it was the following year that legislation was presented in the provincial legislature providing for the deduction of union dues. Many companies have strongly opposed this measure and I have never been able to understand the reasoning they pursue, when it is understood that almost every other conceivable project has been accepted. Many large groups of employees have made declarations to their employers, sometimes without having given notice, requesting that the company make deductions for specific purposes.
In reality the unions are entities and play an important role in our economy. More and more people are coming to realize that unions are an essential part of our economic life. Many large industries now appreciate the importance of the unions in providing bona fide agreements under which the settlement of disputes is simplified, and security and other matters are provided for in writing and followed to the letter. There is every evidence that unions are working in the best interests of everyone concerned.
Despite this increasing recognition of the value of unions, some large corporations still maintain that it is not a part of their social welfare responsibility to make deductions for union dues as they do with regard to other matters. This voluntary revocable check-off represents the very minimum form of union security. I can recall a company with which I negotiated almost going to the point of allowing the operation to be closed down over this very question of accepting the demand for voluntary revocable checkoff. After having accepted the principle of the voluntary revocable check-off the company submitted the question to a board of arbitration, the findings of which were binding on both sides. I believe the chairman

[DOT]of that board of arbitration was Chief Justice Sloan, and the decision of that board has now come to be known as the Sloan formula.
Under the Sloan formula everyone in the bargaining unit is required to pay union dues to the local by which they are represented, whether or not they are members of the organization, and the company is required to deduct union dues from the salary of each employee so designated. There is a slight difference between the Sloan formula and the Rand formula. In the Sloan formula the arbitrator gave the right to those employees who were not members of the union but who were paying union dues to vote on important union questions such as the election of officers. This represented a departure from general procedure, but it was accepted by the union, which felt that those employees who were not registered members of the local but who were paying dues should have some right to determine the course to be followed by the union. This is a form of union security which is certainly a step ahead of the voluntary revocable check-off, and there are many more demanding types of union security with which even many union officers do not agree, such as the closed shop and others.
It has been the argument of the government that the question of voluntary revocable check-off should remain a matter for negotiation. It should be remembered that the questions of wages, job evaluation and the determination of the amount to be paid for each job, are union responsibilities. Many unions have negotiated with employers what is known as job evaluation. Under job evaluation the job carries the rate and the man, woman or juvenile-that would be unusual- would receive that rate of pay. The rates of pay with respect to individuals have been a union-management measure of settlement.
Only last year we brought in legislation providing equal pay for women performing equal work. It could be said also that this should be a matter for discussion between union and management, having regard to what is done in the case of job evaluation. If the legislation concerning equal pay for women performing equal work was good legislation, was legislation that eliminated discrimination, I would point out that these are matters which have been attended to in large measure by way of negotiation. Where there still appears to be some discrimination on the part of employers in what we deem to be a refusal to accept authorization for the deduction of union dues, it would be quite appropriate that this should be covered by legislation of this kind.

I have not a great deal more to say. I have supported this legislation in the past, occasionally to my own embarrassment. Down through the years I have supported it, and I hope the Minister of Labour will see his way clear, if not at this session at least in the near future, to accept this principle of the voluntary revocable check-off.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to speak at length, because my views are well known. May I say to the minister before he speaks that I cannot understand how the federal government can oppose this legislation. Every province in Canada has similar legislation, and there have been no revolutions nor has any province been damaged. We have had it in Nova Scotia since the early part of the century.
We should stop to consider how deeply the federal government are concerned with the check-off. That being so, I cannot see how

Industrial Relations
they can oppose this. I would remind the minister that just recently the Canadian Labour Congress presented a brief in which they asked for the granting of collective bargaining rights to civil servants. According to press reports the Prime Minister said the matter was under consideration. The different civil service associations now enjoy what this bill is asking for; they have a check-off for their dues. In effect these associations are the civil servants' unions.
I caution the minister as to the results if he opposes this bill and then grants collective bargaining rights to the civil service associations. He would then be taking away the right of check-off which they now enjoy. The federal government check off for many things. They check off for income tax, and I do not know how they would get it if they did not. They check off for contributions to the Red Cross and other charitable organizations, and for the purchase of Canada savings bonds.
As far as the rest of CanadJt is concerned, with the exception of our end of the country, the federal government really paved the way for those provinces which have adopted this type of legislation since 1940. The industrial relations committee recommended almost unanimously that this type of check-off be adopted; therefore I urge the minister to support this bill.
The bill would affect only those employed under federal jurisdiction. As I say, all provinces have this type of legislation, some legislation being stronger than others. The provisions of this bill would apply only to crown companies and organizations under the jurisdiction of the federal government. This legislation should have been passed long ago and I do ask the minister to remember that the civil service associations carry out very much the same functions as trade unions, and they now enjoy the check-off. The federal government is considering changing their status and granting them collective bargaining rights.
Unless this bill is passed, unless government employees are to benefit from this type of legislation, which is a form of union security, the civil servants may lose the privilege they now enjoy, not only of having their association dues collected by this method but also contributions toward their large recreational association.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words in connection with the bill introduced by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. I have voted in favour of this bill in the past, and I would like to say a few words in its support. Briefly, of course, labour relations come under provincial jurisdiction for the

most part, excluding those matters which are the concern of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, and they are largely confined to such groups as railway employees, employees of shipping, radio, television and air transport concerns, and those who work for the federal public works department.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 152, REVISED STATUTES OF 1952-VOLUNTARY REVOCABLE CHECK-OFF OF UNION DUES
speechtext:
According to a return tabled on February 8, 1955, there were 392,500 employees under federal jurisdiction, exclusive of civil servants, 277,800 of whom were covered by collective agreements. Of this number 223,400 were covered by the check-off. Therefore only 54,000 employees, or 20 per cent, are not covered by the checkoff. It may be that the number is even less today; certainly there are relatively few employees who are concerned and, as the hon. member for Cape Breton South has just mentioned, civil servants are now covered by a form of check-off. Surely, therefore, it is important as a matter of principle that the voluntary revocable check-off be extended to the remaining federal government employees.
Of course the meaning of the bill in itself is that there is no compulsion here at all. The person concerned has his fees deducted, and at any time he may ask that the union should not receive his fees. In other words this is a voluntary principle, and I think that answers the argument which certain hon. members may put forward, that they do not like the compulsory feature. I do not think there is a compulsory feature in this bill. I may say, Mr. Speaker, that I for one do not see why an employee who does not join a union should receive the protection of the union without paying his fair share. In other words I personally am opposed to the so-called "free-loader".
The other question concerns so-called collective bargaining. Some people would say this should be a matter of collective bargaining, and leave it at that. I wonder how they can say this, after they have thought about it for a minute, because when I am talking about federal employees I am usually talking about employees who are working for crown corporations, for the most part, or for industries which are controlled by the federal government. In other words we are dealing, in a sense, with an emanation of the crown, and surely public policy as well as private policy should be considered. I submit that is another reason why the government should support this bill in principle.
Finally, I may say that this measure has been approved by six provinces, British

Columbia, Saskatchewan, Alberta, Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, and New Brunswick. Of course we are all aware that during wartime there was an order in council

P.C. 1003, I believe-which controlled labour relations and which worked out very satisfactorily. After the war I recall that the national labour code incorporated this principle of the voluntary revocable check-off, until it was deleted by parliament.
I think the time has now come when this clause should be reincorporated into legislation. I think this should be done as a matter of principle, and as a recognition of the role which trade unions play in this country. I, for one, would be very happy to support the bill which has been introduced.

Mr. Speaker, like the sponsor of this Bill No. 4 and those who have spoken in its support this afternoon, I do not propose to take too much of the time of the house, nor do I propose to cover the ground which has been so thoroughly covered over the past several years in the course of arguments both for and against this measure. I must repeat, however, what I have said in more recent years, and that is that the importance of this matter is gradually dwindling in the public mind, not only on the part of the employers but also on the part of the workers, as far as I am able to determine.
I know that my hon. friend who sponsored this bill will have in his office or in his desk three very carefully prepared brochures containing the briefs of the three great labour arganizations, the Canadian Labour Congress, the Canadian and Catholic Confederation of Labour, and the legislative committee of the arotherhoods of the railways. If he has read ;hose briefs this year very carefully, as I am sure he has, he will have found that in none af them has reference been made to the voluntary revocable check-off or to check-off af any kind.
Mr. Speaker, in saying that I must be aerfectly fair and state, too, that one of the 'entlemen presenting his congress' brief last week interjected these words into the midst
Industrial Relations
of the reading. He said-and it would not be stating the case fairly if I did not refer to this interjection:
I would like to say a word here about check-off of dues. This is a very important question which was overlooked in preparing the document which is now in front of you. My face is certainly a little red at the moment, and I do not mean com-munistically.
Mr. Speaker, I do not mean in any sense to try to lessen the importance of this measure in the minds of hon. members of this house. It is an important matter even though its importance now in the federal field is certainly not equal to the importance it had even as late as 1953. My hon. friend from Cape Breton South has said that the civil service associations would lose the rights they now possess to have membership dues deducted at the source if such a measure as this were not passed. That would not happen at all. Whatever rights these associations have with regard to the deduction of their dues were arrived at by discussion and negotiation on the part of their authorized representatives at the time they made the arrangements with regard to them, and as they go on to enter new discussions or new negotiations, whatever you may call them, they will be quite free, as crown companies have been free, to utilize the check-off in some form or other as a factor in the negotiations.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I would like to put on record the results of a survey of the numbers employed under federal jurisdiction who are affected by the check-off or who might be affected by this measure introduced by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre; and since this is a fairly long schedule I would like to suggest, if I have the unanimous consent of the house, that I place it on Hansard and have the situation brought up to date.

In order that this may have some meaning, may I point out that it will be seen that a total of approximately 395,700 persons are employed in industries which come under federal jurisdiction. This total, of course, includes crown companies. It does not include classified civil servants. This figure should be reduced by a total of approximately 100,800 employees who do not come within the scope of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act and comprise managers, supervisory employees or others who are employed in banks or in some government enterprises where employees are not yet organized and are not covered by collective agreements.

Of the remaining 294,900 employees who are employed in industries where there is an established pattern of organized bargaining, the table shows that 289,500 are covered by collective agreements. Of this total, 230,300 are covered by agreements which have some form of check-off. In other words approximately 80 per cent of the employees who are covered by collective agreements have the check-off in some form or other. It is also revealing to know that of the 230,300 employees who have some form of check-off, only 44,600 are subject to the voluntary-revocable check-off.
That brings the record up to date, and it is a little different from what it was a year

ago. The remaining 81 per cent were covered by check-offs of one kind or another-the Rand formula has been mentioned-which the employees concerned apparently felt were of more value to them than the voluntary revocable check-off.
I have been accused of bringing forward the argument from year to year that this is a matter that should be dealt with by collective bargaining, and I feel that is true. We have had a great deal of discussion in the last few weeks about what should happen with respect to collective bargaining in the federal field. I believe that in that field the policy of the government should be more and more to promote that kind of climate which will encourage responsible and healthy industrial relations.
We have some small element of compulsion in our Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. We say that certain conciliation procedures shall take place. We say that every collective agreement for a term of less than one year or for an indeterminate term will be looked upon as being for a term of one year. Those are points which have compulsory features, but they are quite different from what is contained in the bill. They help to make up that framework in which collective bargaining can be well and effectively carried out, and the moment parliament begins to legislate even in a small way in favour of one side of the bargaining table and does not provide something of an equivalent nature for the other side, then I contend we are taking unto ourselves some of those matters that are important in reaching a sound and useful agreement between the two parties concerned.
While the Minister of Labour and the government are in favour of union security, and are in favour of the principle contained here when it is reached by collective bargaining, for the reasons I have given I will vote against the bill today as I did last year. Many of the crown companies referred to now have some kind of check-off, but they have achieved it with the tacit agreement of the government. They have achieved it through collective bargaining and so should those very few others who desire it and who come under federal jurisdiction.

To authorize payments to the national conference of Canadian universities (hereinafter called "the conference") for the purpose of making grants to institutions of higher learning in accordance with an agreement entered into or to be entered into, with the approval of the governor in council, between the Minister of Finance and the conference, such agreement to include, inter alia, provision that the total amount of grants to all the institutions of higher learning in any one province be calculated by multiplying the population of the province by $1, and that any amount payable to an institution of higher learning and not paid by the conference in the present fiscal year may be retained by the conference until such time as the institution to which the money is payable claims the payment from the conference or parliament provides otherwise for the disposal thereof; the amount appropriated under vote 132 of the Appropriation Act No. 6, 1956 to be applied to the purposes of this vote; additional amount required, $7,986,000.

Mr. Chairman, before recess I was stating my opposition to this item although, like other members of the house, I recognize the difficulties faced by Canadian universities. Quebec universities face such difficulties as do those of other provinces, and provincial governments have to make 82715-49J

great efforts to help them. For its part, the Quebec government is making a tremendous effort in that field in authorizing an expenditure of nearly 82 million dollars over a period of 12 years; to help universities. However, I realize like the other members that even this effort is not sufficient to solve all the problems which beset our universities.
I do not think that we can solve the problem by creating other problems, and the measure now being considered is a clumsy measure, one which leans towards centralization.
The government can certainly not claim this to be a very great find, since this formula is unacceptable not only to the Quebec provincial government but also to the universities of that province. It seems to me that surely the government could have found a more readily acceptable solution to the problem. I think that the difficulty is that the people of my province, at any rate, are simply convinced that this proposal is but another step, on the part of the federal government towards centralization, a centralization which has intensified since the war.
True, this afternoon, the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) did point out other spheres of activity upon which the federal government had encroached without eliciting any protests from the provinces. However, in most cases, the provinces could not do otherwise. Education, though, is another matter since this is a field which is basically provincial. As the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) said yesterday, if education had not been reserved to the provinces, the British North America Act would never have been ratified and confederation would never have come about. Our constitution would not have been accepted if education had not been protected by those very clear sections of that pact.
Besides, only the provinces are in a position to face the technical problems of education, having departments of education whose officials have the experience required to deal with matters of such complexity. We, in Quebec, who constitute the French minority of this country, feel that the sections of the constitution dealing with education are the most vital ones, and that, in this respect, we cannot yield any ground.
If the federal government is now offering those grants to universities, it is simply because, with the amount of income tax it is collecting, it has accumulated huge surpluses and the federal government alone can afford to be generous in fields of activity from which, according to the constitution, it is barred.

I am not surprised that some people are asking, as was done yesterday in this house, for grants to assist elementary education, because, among all governments, the federal government is the only one with such money surpluses, and is the only one which could afford the luxury of invading fields of activity from which it has been excluded by the constitution.
The federal government has such surpluses simply because it taxes too heavily. I therefore would suggest that the best way for the present government to assist in the field of education at every level, and particularly to assist universities which need it so badly, is to give up a part of its taxation fields. This year, its surplus might run close to 700 million-

-unless it finds ways to hand money around, so it will not have to blush about all that accumulated money derived from its reckless taxation over the last four years.
I know that my colleagues from other provinces who are not as scrupulous or as touchy as I am, because they do not belong to a minority, are ready to welcome that federal assistance to universities, because they are thinking only of the problems of those institutions. This is also the case of other provincial governments and universities in other provinces which are also prepared to accept federal grants and even urge that they be made larger.
Consequently, I do not want to insist that the universities of other provinces be penalized, but I do not believe that Quebec itself should be penalized because it attaches greater importance to the constitution than do the other provinces. Therefore, I ask the federal government to add an income tax deductibility clause proportionate to the amount which the Quebec institutions would have received if they all had accepted the offer of the federal government. The deductibility has already been considered in the past for other reasons, and I believe it might be possible in this way to help universities without encroaching upon the constitution.
In this way the concern shown by the government and Quebec institutions for the letter of the constitution would be respected, and all the universities of this country would be treated on an equal basis.
Without the addition of such a section, and in its present form, I believe that the item now under consideration is unacceptable. Consequently, I will have to vote against this item.

Mr. Chairman, first I would like to join those who have complimented the Prime Minister upon the realistic speech on this subject he made this afternoon. I should like also to mention the fact that during this session, particularly the last couple of weeks, the question of education has received a lot of attention from all quarters. This indicates that the problem is becoming a pertinent one in all provinces.
While we welcome the increase in the grants to the provinces, as far as I am concerned, coming from Nova Scotia, I want to indicate that this does not eliminate the fact that we are below the other provinces in the grant per student. I shall say more about this later, but I would just like to mention the fact, that in Nova Scotia we elected a new government recently, and the premier of that province is also the minister of education. They have not, so far, held a session of the legislature, but I have read a statement he made to the press that so far as that province was concerned their policy with respect to education was retrenchment; in other words, they could not continue to pour the money into education that is, perhaps, needed, because they do not have it.
Second, he said, grants to the municipalities were to be curtailed. This indicates that as far as education is concerned that province is in great difficulties. I am not quarrelling with the statement made by the premier of Nova Scotia, but I would point out that in the speech from the throne in the province of Ontario, where the government is of the same complexion, much additional expenditure on education is forecast, together with increased expenditure on such ancillaries to education as assistance to the municipalities, the building of schools and so forth. So the matter is not a political one; it is an economic question.
In every second newspaper one picks up there seems to be a statement by some eminent person on the present requirements of education and its future needs. Only this afternoon I was reading in the Ottawa Journal the report of a speech by Mr. Crump, of the C.P.R., in which he pointed out the growing need for teachers and staff in the universities. He stressed that the salaries of university teachers should be increased by 100 per cent in order to make the vocation more attractive to entrants, and to hold those for whom industry may be fishing. Of course these statements go on to forecast what the student population will be

10 years from now, and to emphasize the need for funds in order to expand facilities for accommodating these students. The fact of the matter is that according to the forecast the number will be doubled, and it all adds up to the need for more money.
Now, Mr. Chairman, with provincial incomes as they are today, there is no possibility, with the system of straight grants, of getting equality in education as between province and province. The federal government will, in my judgment have to take a greater interest and provide more funds in future if we are to meet the requirements of the universities. When I say that, I realize the difficulties with which the federal government has to contend. The British North America Act makes education the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces, and any changes with respect to entering this field, financially or otherwise, have to be made by agreement with the province or by changes in the act itself. I think it is time the provincial governments, if they are all Canadian and if they want equality of opportunity as between province and province, will have to begin to realize that they are living in 1957, not in 1867, and changed conditions will have to be brought about.
I have argued from time to time in this house that rather than the grant being made to a university on the basis of the number of students in that university, the fact that it is related to the population works a hardship on some of the provinces which are not so wealthy, and I have suggested from time to time that grants should be made on the basis of the student population. In other words the number of students in the university should be the guide as to the amount of the grant.
Since this matter was last discussed in the house some of our people have been doing some "homework". Getting the figures, province by province, with respect to the student population as related to the general population in the particular province, or the number of students from other provinces who are in the universities of a neighbouring province, was not easy. The figures go back pretty far; they go back to 1951 and 1952, and the best examples we could find were put on record by the Minister of Finance on August 14, 1956. They are in Hansard at page 7591. The minister sets out there the grant per student from province to province, and I am just going to recite these figures for the purpose of my argument.
In Newfoundland the grant per student was $357.64; in Prince Edward Island, $207.69; in New Brunswick, $112.36; Ontario, $137.84;
Supply-Finance
Manitoba, $101.55; Saskatchewan, $151.97; Alberta, $149.80; British Columbia, $99.42; Nova Scotia, $80.85.
These figures, the latest we could get, show definitely that Nova Scotia is away below all the other provinces. The reason for that is, of course, that the student population of the universities in relation to the population of that province is so much higher than in the other provinces. That situation arises because the province of Nova Scotia has facilities for the study of such subjects as medicine and dentistry, which do not exist in the other maritime provinces. Thus a large number of students from Newfoundland, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island who require this type of training are obliged to go to Nova Scotia in order to enter these particular fields, with the result that in the matter of grants Nova Scotia is being penalized because it was farsighted enough to establish the facilities which were required in that part of the country for instruction in these professions.
I have argued from time to time that the grants should be made by reference to the size of the student body and without reference to the population figure; but after looking over this matter with some of our experts I find that this suggestion, if applied literally as I have presented it in the past, would result in hardship to other provinces. The other three maritime provinces, Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick and Newfoundland, would lose considerably by an arrangement of that kind. That would also be true of Alberta, Manitoba and Saskatchewan. They would lose; and as far as I am concerned and, I think, as far as the people of Nova Scotia are concerned, we are not prepared to do injury to any other province in order to better our own position.
We have come to the conclusion-and when I say "we" I mean the members of this group who have been studying the question-that it is not good enough just to argue against something; there should be some alternative proposal, and I think the fairest solution we could arrive at would be one which recognized the fact that Nova Scotia is in her present position because she provided facilities which are being made use of by students from neighbouring provinces, where the opportunity for such studies does not at present exist.
Instead of a formula whereby the grant is made on the basis of the student population, we felt it would be fairer to suggest to the government that in the circumstances in which that province finds itself or, for that matter, if any other province finds itself in a similar position in the not too

Supply-Finance
distant future, the government should consider, in addition to the grants now provided under the present formula which results in Nova Scotia definitely being placed at a great disadvantage, the possibility of establishing under the Canada Council additional grants to universities providing the type of education that has resulted in Nova Scotia finding herself in the position in which she is today. Such additional grants should be provided to schools which are turning out specialists where such schools are not available in other provinces.
I leave that thought with the Prime Minister because I do not believe he, the government or anyone else who has given any thought to the matter would want to continue to keep that province in its present position of, on the one hand, providing the facilities and accepting students from all over the country and, on the other hand, being so low down in the scale so far as grants to the universities are concerned. I think the matter calls for some additional thinking and some special arrangement on the part of the government to assist schools that are providing such special training. There should be an additional grant to enable them to expand in the future without the handicap from which they are now suffering.
Of course, education is going to cost a great deal of money. If the forecasts the experts are making today are correct, then the amount of money that will be needed for capital expansion of the universities, which are expected to have double the present student population in 10 or 15 years time, will mean that someone else is going to have to help to share the burden.
I have heard it stated on many occasions in the house that the U.S.S.R. is far ahead of Canada and the United States with respect to education. I have said before and I repeat that we must remember that in that country there are no companies, corporations or anyone else making any money. The profits that go to private industry in this country go to the state in Russia, and the state uses them for whatever purpose it wishes. They are pouring a lot of money into education, and if we are going to meet that challenge I think industries making fair profits in Canada will have to begin to think in terms of endowment funds for universities in order to enable us to meet the educational needs of the future.
Recently I noticed that some of the big companies are making pretty substantial contributions to some of our universities. I hope they will continue to do so, because with our population, the need of education as indicated

by everyone who speaks on the subject, and the huge sums of money required, we cannot keep on dumping the cost on the taxpayers all the time because many taxpayers can ill afford the taxes they are paying today. But I do think that corporations making profits running into the hundreds of millions might very well consider it a good insurance policy for the future to assist in meeting the huge outlays that are going to be necessary in the field of education in the future. In my opinion they should look upon it as one of the best forms of insurance available to them to guarantee that the system under which they now operate and the freedom they enjoy will continue to be moulded to a considerable extent by the architects of the future, the citizens of this continent. That does not only apply to universities but also to primary education.
I hope the Prime Minister and particularly the Minister of Finance will give some consideration to the proposal that there should be an additional grant payable to universities in some provinces which are providing certain types of education that are not available in other provinces.

Mr. Chairman, along with other members of this group who have already expressed their opinions may I say I listened with a great deal of interest to the words of the Prime Minister this afternoon when speaking on this subject. From what he said I believe we can come to the conclusion that he has quite a good grasp of the need to deal with the crisis in university education.
He emphasized, and I think all of us could bear this in mind, that one of the first requirements to improve the status of university education is to see that the professors and other teachers in these institutions of higher learning receive adequate salaries. Until people throughout the nation generally recognize that our university teachers are performing services on a par with the most valuable service performed by other Canadians, and recognize that fact by way of adequate salary schedules, we will continue to debate the subject of a crisis in our institutions of higher learning.
From what little study I have made of the problem it seems that we have been slipping over the years. In the 1920's it is probable that in relation to the needs of the country at that time we were farther ahead than we are today. I have noticed figures indicating that in 1926 grants from governments generally to universities were 130 per cent greater than the cost to the university students. By 1950 grants from governments to universities were only 10 per cent in

excess of the cost to the students. Following a contribution by the people of Canada through an item of some $7 million in the estimates the gap was partially closed, and it is estimated that with the item under discussion we shall be approximately back to the 1926 position in this regard.
It seems to me that if we are to meet the need of our universities brought about by the natural increase in enrolment resulting from our growing population and the need for greater numbers of university graduates, we as a nation are going to have to raise our sights. The Financial Post gave a good deal of attention to this subject in its issue of August 25, 1956. In an article in that issue Mr. Burke Stannard points out the large sums of money that will be needed in the future to take care of education in our country. He points out that while today we are spending approximately $800 million per year on education at all levels, this amount will require to be increased to $15 billion spread over the next ten years; and that if university enrolment increases to 300,000 the amount of $15,120 million will need to be increased to $17,500 million. Therefore any additional expenditure passed by the house at this time is a small sum in relation to this very large undertaking.	'
I have in my hand a statement giving amounts to be spent by various levels of government on education in this country- these are estimates-for the fiscal year 195556. They were prepared by the federal government some time ago for discussions with the provinces. These figures show that the federal government in that year would spend approximately $25 million in grants to education of all types; that the provincial governments of this nation would spend just under $300 million and that the municipalities, the local levels of government, would spend approximately $457 million, making total expenditures in this nation for that period of time of some $782 million.
If one breaks down those figures on a percentage basis, then to each education dollar the federal government is now contributing at the rate of 3 cents; the provinces combined are contributing 38 cents, and the municipalities and school districts, the local levels of government, are providing 58 cents. Even if as a result of this and other action the expenditure of $25 million by the federal government should be increased to $40 million, then the federal percentage would be up to only 5 per cent. If, as we hope, along with increased expenditures by the federal government, there will be increased expenditures by provincial
Supply-Finance
governments and undoubtedly by governments at the municipal level, then the federal percentage may drop back again to near the current rate of just 3 per cent.
I think Mr. James S. Duncan, former president and general manager of the Massey-Harris-Ferguson corporation, has performed a useful service for the people of Canada in the study he has given to the educational system of our country and the educational systems and their results in other nations in the world. I think Canada's record is something of which no member of this house is proud, because not a member of this house can be proud of the comparison, having regard to the emphasis we are placing on education in this country compared to what is being done in the United States or in the U.S.S.R.
This evening we are discussing the passing of this further supplementary estimate. The Financial Post of the same date points out that for each 1,000 of population in Canada there are just 4.94 students enrolled in universities. In the United States the figure is 15. In the U.S.S.R. the figure is 19.6. Mr. Duncan and others have pointed out how necessary it will be to the future technological development of this country that we close soon at least a substantial part of this gap. It has already been pointed out that in 1954 in Russia there were graduated some 53,000 engineers. In the United States in the same year there were graduated just 23,000 engineers. In Canada the figure is running at approximately 2,000 engineers per year.
Some may say that our engineers have a broader education. That is probably true. Some may think they are even better qualified in a very specialized field. But here again it is pointed out that the graduate engineer in the Soviet union has spent 50 per cent more study hours than has an engineer in the United States, and I presume the same statement would apply to Canada. Of the engineers graduated in the United States, experience has shown that some 35 per cent are lost to engineering because they go into some other profession. Hence even these figures do not show the true preponderance in the engineers that are available to industry in the Soviet union as compared with the number available to industry in the United States.
I notice some amazing figures of the number of medical doctors being graduated. According to these figures, in 1955 the Soviet union graduated 27,000 medical doctors as compared to 7,000 in the United States. We graduate approximately 900 per year. Surely the medical field is deserving of greater effort by the people of Canada. I am afraid that

when the Soviet union has this great preponderance in graduate engineers, medical men and scientists, they may make available such a large number to assist underdeveloped countries that, by comparison, in this field also we may be far behind.
Mr. Duncan says that the U.S.S.R. in 1955 graduated 120,000 scientists and engineers, against the figure of 70,000 in the United States. Of course Russia is attempting to build her nation as the technological capital of the world, as the area of the world with the greatest number of scientists and skilled professional people. Because she is graduating such a large number of scientists and is so determined to out-bid the western world, one finds that Russia is now undertaking very substantial loans to underdeveloped countries. Mr. Philander P. Claxton, Jr., special assistant to the assistant secretary for congressional relations, points out that $1-3 billion is being made available by the Soviet union by way of low-interest loans to assist 11 underdeveloped countries.
I am sure Canadians generally feel that we in this nation must come to grips with the question of the crisis in higher education; and that if this government takes the lead, as it now appears to be doing, the day will and must come when this great difference between what we are accomplishing and what is being accomplished in other nations is overcome. I look forward to the day when every young Canadian who has the ability to take advantage of a university education will have that opportunity irrespective of the amount of money that his parents, relatives or friends may be able to advance to him toward that end. I believe that we in this nation must work toward the time when Canadians have this opportunity. If they have the opportunity-irrespective of their individual ability to pay at the moment-of obtaining a university education, I am sure we will lead in this field.

While listening very carefully to the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer), I was under the impression that, besides representing here a federal constituency the hon. member was also a spokesman for the provincial government. Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent)

who is as free to introduce it as we are free to accept or reject it. As far and as long as there is no encroachment upon any section of the British North America Act, I will not hesitate to approve the item now submitted to the house by the right hon. Prime Minister and the members of his cabinet.
If the British North America Act were threatened, the Prime Minister would not have considered the matter now before the house and I can say quite clearly, that no government could induce me to vote in favor of such a measure. I am a good Canadian; I live in the province of Quebec and I mean to be a Canadian citizen in the full sense of that word since I have the honour to sit in the parliament of a country made up of ten provinces. It is only right that we should be interested in our own province but we must also, as a matter of principle, show some interest for anything which may happen in other provinces.
I noticed that, in his remarks, the hon. member for Three Rivers has said that the house was being presented with a clumsy measure.

He is the one who is
clumsy.

But, Mr. Chairman, I must say that I do not share his opinion. The hon. member has adopted an attitude which I am at a loss to understand.
I have had more than one opportunity to discuss this matter with a certain number of people and never have I met anybody, outside of political life, who has not recognized that this proposal was the best solution that the Prime Minister could adopt in order to make peace between the province of Quebec and the other provinces and ensure the respect of the privileges of all the provinces.
Since the hon. member is now at his desk, Mr. Chairman, I want to say to him that he could have talked about the grants which the provincial government does accept. He could have told us if the construction of vocational schools by the Liberal government in the province of Quebec, 50 per cent of the cost of these schools having been met by the federal government, has meant any lessening of the rights of the provinces in educational matters?
Since that time Mr. Duplessis has come into power and a number of similar schools have been built with federal and provincial funds. Has this step meant that a single boy or girl or even a single teacher has changed his or her way of thinking, has become anglicized or anything of the sort? I have never heard it said, and I do not believe that anything like that has ever happened.

It is an admitted fact that we have several provinces, whose approach to various matters can differ, but it is high time that we should be able to discuss national interest with frankness without being told we are encroaching upon the authority of the provincial governments, whether it be that of Ontario or that of Quebec. We sit here as representatives of the country as a whole; we represent ten provinces and not one.
We must protect the interests of the ten provinces while safeguarding the rights granted the citizens of Quebec by the British North America Act. I am sure that no one would want to violate the British North America Act because, if this should happen, it would mean war and I would be the first one to shed my blood in the defence of my fellow citizens.
If there has been no change since the building of the vocational schools was started, and if the Prime Minister gives me the assurance that the grants will be distributed to the universities by an independent council of the federal government, I wonder why some would make petty politics out of it while pretending to defend interests which do not exist.
As I say, I am a Canadian and I challenge anyone to say that I have not always done my duty in whatever field it be. I have read the bill several times, as many times as did the hon. member. I am not a lawyer but I have more confidence in a man whose competence is certainly as great as that of the hon. member for Three Rivers, and I refer to the Prime Minister. Both belong to the legal profession, and if the Prime Minister had thought for a moment that the measure would be harmful to the province of Quebec, I am sure that he would not have submitted it.
Mr. Chairman, I do not want to speak too long on this matter but, as the hon. member for Three Rivers is back in his seat, I want to tell him that we are good friends but also that we are here to speak our minds. I like to believe that he is sincere as I am myself. For twelve years I sat on the council of my municipality and not one of my fellow councillors can say that I even once mixed provincial politics with municipal administration, whether under the Duplessis or the Godbout administration. Not only that, but I asserted the rights of my municipality, under the Godbout administration, which was Liberal, and I even asserted them under the Duplessis regime, as I was a member of the council until 1950.
In proposing this measure, the government shows a remarkable broadness of outlook. Yet, there is still opposition to it.

Mr. Chairman, I am glad the supplementary estimate of the Prime Minister regarding aid to universities is now before the committee, so I may say a few words on behalf of the universities. We are living in a remarkable era in Canadian development; it does not require any great knowledge of history to recognize this fact, and we are prepared to admit it without argument. The evidence is somewhat more striking in some parts of the country than

Supply-Finance
in others, but there is scarcely a community in which people are not conscious of it. It is not only that the great cities are becoming monstrous in size and the smaller cities are astonishing themselves with their growth, but the quiet countrysides are being uprooted. In remote areas from Labrador to Aklavik which have lain undisturbed century after century the age-old remains of the glaciers are being rudely pushed aside by bulldozers.
Let me remind the committee of that period from 1900 to 1913 which came under the direction of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, the prime minister who said, and believed, that the twentieth century belongs to Canada. During this period the rate of growth was even greater than it has been in the last decade. The relative increase in population was greater, and the number of immigrants reached very much higher figures. We then received from abroad relatively much higher these facts to the attention of the committee imports of capital than we do now. I recall because we have a tendency to forget our history. However, we have to admit that under the Prime Minister and his leadership the whole Canadian nation is on the move.
There is one thing we need to remember if we are to see our own time in proper perspective. Because our school histories tell us that the settlement of Canada began at Port Royal in 1603 or at Quebec in 1608 we can appreciate that the experiment in colonizing this northern half of the continent has been going on for about 350 years. It began at least as early as the settlement of the United States, and one might argue that it began a year or two earlier. We tend to forget in our present excitement just how long we and former generations of Canadians have been engaged in the business of developing Canada. We are prone to forget what long periods of waiting and discouragement there have been in our history. We are inclined to ignore questions as to why development in the United States has been much more rapid.
Generally speaking, the experience of history yields the very clear conclusion that the kind of resources we have in Canada, rendered less accessible by climate and dispersed population, made it necessary to wait until the western world had developed an industrial civilization with the need for our resources and with the technical means of uncovering and exploiting them. This was

what was in the mind of Sir Wilfrid Laurier when he said that the twentieth century belonged to Canada. He obviously did not mean that other countries had not a share in it. Having the whole history of this country in his blood and anticipating the long periods of waiting, he meant that the seventeenth, eighteenth and nineteenth centuries had passed Canada by in a certain measure, but that she would enter the full stream of world development in the twentieth century.
Until about 40 years ago, save for the closed chapter of the fur trade, Canadian development had been largely the application of industry to limited resources similar to those of the United States. Our farming areas in the east were similar to those in the eastern part of the United States. Our prairies were just the last of the North American prairies. Forestry was no different in Maine, Michigan and Washington from what it was in New Brunswick, Ontario and British Columbia. Our mining was an extension of United States mining. When we became engaged in the automobile industry Windsor and Oshawa were just much smaller versions of Detroit and Flint.
Today our current economic developments are much more distinctive. Despite large investments of United States capital many of our developments have a recognizably Canadian colour. At least some of the resources now being developed are distinctively Canadian. There is also apparent in this country a buoyant spirit of confidence and initiative and a sense of pride in what is Canadian. This notable period of national development has been stimulated by a coincidence of favourable influences. Our ship has moved out of the shallows; wind, tide and current speed us on our way.
One thing which has happened is that with the great spread and expansion of industry throughout the world and particularly in the United States the industrial intake of materials and particularly of metals and energy has increased enormously. It seems almost impossible to fill the machines which we have created with the amount and variety of materials they demand. With industrialization has come, also, a phenomenal increase in urbanization, in city and suburban living. On this continent this seems in part to be based on the greater economy of purchasing services, for example frozen foods and automatic dishwashers, as opposed

to hiring services in the form of domestic and other help. Cost has forced us to get our services from the factory.
As industry multiplies and cities spread, new methods have become available for the discovery and exploitation of natural resources. The aeroplane has replaced the canoe in transporting the prospector. A whole series of instruments ranging from magnetometers to geiger counters can discover beneath heavy overburden the likely places for drilling. Modern earth-moving equipment has made possible exploitation with a speed which would have been incredible even 25 years ago. Changing methods of manufacture and use have given special importance to light metals, chemicals and synthetics, and the use of power, other than from coal, just at the time when we were tapping our oil resources and were capable of developing the last and remote sources of waterpower.
In the changes that are taking place capital and industrial knowledge from the United States are playing an important part, but though United States capital has been of decisive significance in many industries, it has in the over-all picture supplied not more than about 15 per cent of the total investment. Along with these revolutionary changes there has come, of course, growth in all sorts of other industries and areas for which these changes have created larger markets and more profitable opportunities for investment.
One of the most notable features of this period of our growth has been its persistence. Beginning as a period of active reconstruction, it proceeded through the Korean war boom, ran through two mild recessions, and in the past few months has shown remarkable vigour and expansive power. Ultimately the Conservatives and the C.C.F.'ers, the type of people who refer to the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce as an optimist and who continually predict that the boom will come to an end, assuredly will be right; but so far the fulfilment of their predictions has been postponed year by year.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
As the hon. member has been interrupted, I think perhaps I should point out to him that we are discussing one 82715-50J
