specific item in the supplementary estimates. I have no desire to stop the hon. member laying such foundation as he thinks necessary to lay in order to discuss the item, but we are discussing solely a vote of some $7 million to be made under certain circumstances to universities. I think I should ask the hon. member to come to the point of the resolution with reasonable speed.

I am just laying the foundation as to why it is necessary to assist the universities. It has now become a sort of national occupation to attempt to predict what the national product of this country will be in 10 or 20 years' time, or to stake one's reputation upon the prediction that the population will be 22 million or 25 million by 1975.
With these industrial changes has come a great increase in population, helped by moderate immigration but arising mainly from a high birth rate. We have to cope at present with a population which has in it an unusually large number of children and a growing proportion of older, retired people. The number of dependents per income earner is at present abnormally large. In a few years, however, this will begin to change, as a larger number of the children born since 1945 or a little earlier enter the working force.
One of the interesting things that is happening is that because of resources and power and with the help of more effective transportation, a number of great industries are being established much further to the north than hitherto. Areas unfit for agriculture and producing little in the way of forest wealth have become the base for large industries. One of the constricting factors in our history hitherto has been the irregular, thin band of population never more than a few hundred miles from the United States border. It seems possible that we are now developing much more in depth, and much more in those parts of the country which are peculiarly and exclusively Canadian. There is here an interesting basis for conjecture for all who are concerned about the gradual development of distinctive Canadian characteristics in our culture and way of life.
All this is a pleasant, rather exhilarating success story, in which there have been relatively few disappointments and surprisingly few delays. True, the growth has brought with it difficult and wearisome problems of enlarging our living space and extending the whole apparatus of transportation and community living. Whether these problems involve gas pipe lines, a new and mammoth highway system or the provision of sewers and waters for swollen urban populations, the federal, provincial and municipal governments are wearily grappling with problems of

Supply-Finance
growth, and are concerned with many others with which they have not yet come to grips.
We are stimulated by the experience of our material progress, and we are engrossed with the problems of resources, transportation and the capital investment which confront us. I am not one who deprecates either the importance of material progress or the sense of achievement which goes with the conversion of the forces of nature to man's purposes. The sense of achievement in mastering and using resources is something that goes deep into the consciousness of the people who have confronted this problem for the past 300 years.
We are spending enormous sums in the development of our material resources, and already we are beginning to ask ourselves searching questions as to whether we are giving enough attention to the conservation of our sources of pulp and metals, oil and gas and water. We are asking ourselves whether in the physical development of our country we are becoming more Canadian, and whether we are making it more worth-while to be a Canadian.
As soon as we look beyond the stock market and beyond the pressing daily problems that confront us, we all know that these material resources and the great industries and cities which are being built up will in themselves neither create a distinctive Canada nor make it a truly great nation. We may acquire something which imitates other countries, or might have been made from a department store pattern. There are, however, resources which are more important than oil, metals, spruce and water. They call for the boldest investment; they require the shrewdest selection; they need the most thrifty and long-sighted conservation. It is the human resources of a nation which give it distinction and guarantee its future.
Thus I am pleased that the Prime Minister has introduced a bill which will assist the universities in developing the people of this country so they can use the great natural resources which we have in such large quantities. It is the people who will put to work the things God has given to this country, who will help Canada take its place as a first-class power in the world.

Will the Prime Minister bring us up to date concerning the situation with regard to engineers and scientists? We all realize that this vote provides for payments without any conditions direct to universities, but we hear most alarming reports from time to time about the great shortage of scientists and engineers. For example, there was a report published last week by the Engineering Institute of Canada with reference to the

alarming current and prospective shortage of Canadian engineers and scientists. This paragraph appeared in the press report:
More words have been spoken and printed about this situation than about almost anything else. Many voices have proclaimed the urgency, but after years of talk no one has done anything of consequence that will improve the situation quickly.
And again:
There is some promise now that government and industry will help, but the needs appear to be away beyond any sums that are being mentioned as available shortly.
We all know how important scientists and engineers are to Canada at present and in the years immediately ahead. Can the Prime Minister tell us what is the opinion of the government with regard to all this talk of an acute shortage, and if there is such a shortage whether any steps are being taken to meet it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I cannot give any precise figures to the hon. gentleman. At the present time there are indications of intentions to provide structures of various kinds to a total amount that would be beyond the capabilities of the available scientific or engineering or skilled or unskilled manpower, and greater than the materials available. There is a certainty that not everything can be accomplished that Canadians and Canadian corporations would like to do or have expressed intentions of trying to do during 1957.
Because of the shortage of trained men?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Because the total is greater than the population of this country, with its savings and even the savings that come from abroad, with its manpower and its materials, can realize in the one year. During last year I understand the amount of capital investment was of the order of about $7.75 billion. Estimates that have been gathered for what I believe are called intentions for the present year would indicate an increase of as much as 12J per cent over what was realized in 1956. Of course that would not necessarily be 12J per cent in actual volume because there is an expectation that prices over the year in the construction trades-the capital investment trades- are apt to be as much as 5 per cent higher than in 1956. That would still leave an actual physical increase of 7J per cent over what was realized in 1956, and my information from the data available to our experts, and their best estimates, is that this is more than the economy can produce.
Now, with respect to the so-called shortage of engineers, I know there is a greater demand for engineers than there was when

either the hon. gentleman or I were at university. Just as one illustration of what I have in mind let me mention this. The hon. gentleman knows the reputation of the Taschereau family in the province of Quebec; it was always producing either clergymen or lawyers or judges. That family has supplied Canada with a number of very distinguished clergymen. The first cardinal was a Taschereau. They have supplied a number of very distinguished judges, and a still larger number of brilliant members of the bar in the province of Quebec. A Taschereau was my partner when I was at the bar. He has only one son, and the son, instead of following in his father's footsteps as has been done for generations by male members of that family, is studying to be an engineer.
This is because there is now a realization among the young people that there is a greater demand for engineers, and consequently there are more young people adopting that vocation than formerly. I feel, therefore, that there will be a greater number of engineers in the future. There will be a greater demand upon the universities to train engineers, and I know that right here in Ottawa there has been a very substantially filled subscription list in response to an invitation to Quebec and Ontario industrialists to contribute to the establishment of an engineering faculty at the University of Ottawa. They are doing this because they feel their businesses will require that kind of equipment. It is just as essential to their businesses to have trained staff as it is to have the machines which they instal in their plants. It is, I think, a very encouraging sign that our industrialists should be realizing, as I said a moment ago, that the greatest of our natural resources are our human resources, and that these human resources have to be developed and cultivated if we want to make full use of the other material resources with which our land is blessed.
I do not wish to expand upon that subject, but I do wish to answer, or try to answer, four questions which were submitted by the hon. member for Cariboo. As for the first question, I am not in a position to answer it with accurate statistical information. The hon. member inquired whether $1 per capita would represent, now, the same proportion of university expenditure as 50 cents per capita represented in 1951. I think it would, perhaps, represent rather more than the same proportion, because I do not think there has been an increase of 100 per cent since 1951 in university expenditures.
The second question was, why are these grants not just turned over to the provincial governments? Well, the equalization
Supply-Finance
grants will be turned over to the provincial governments, but the provincial governments have a great many calls upon their finances, and these grants are recommended to parliament so they may go to the universities and to no other quarter; and we think that by placing them in the hands of the national conference of Canadian universities they will go to those universities. There may be other very desirable purposes to which these amounts could be applied if they were just handed over for general application by the provincial governments, but I think it is the desire of most members of this house that these grants should go specifically to the universities.
The third question was, will the grants be free of restriction with regard to curricula, salaries and so forth? The federal government does not wish to establish any kind of control over the freedom of the universities. The amounts are to be turned over to the national council and, in turn, by the national council to the particular institutions which are recognized by the provincial governments as being of university level, and I am confident that the authorities in those university institutions will make good use of the money available.
I think it would be an attempt to exercise some jurisdiction over educational affairs to tell the council that it might, as our agent, say to them what the curricula of their studies should be. That is something which is within provincial jurisdiction and which should remain within provincial jurisdiction.
Another question was, would it be possible for this aid to constitute a sort of revolving fund which beneficiaries would return to the university in order that it might be used to help other promising students to whom it might be of use. Well, the amounts are not very considerable with respect to each individual university, but if a university chose to use the whole of what it received, or a certain portion of that amount, for the purpose of making advances to promising students on the understanding that the amount would be returned, that would be something which would be quite within the discretion of the university concerned to decide. All we are asking parliament to do is to say that the government of Canada should contribute to the work of the universities an annual sum of the order, at the present time, of about $16 million a year, or $1 per head of the Canadian population, and distribute it in proportion to the population of each province, as between the provinces, and in proportion to the student enrolment within each province.
In that respect, the hon. member for Cape Breton South-he is not here at the moment

Supply-Finance
-recited figures that were put on record in Hansard last August. But I am informed that those figures do not tell the whole story. I am not making any assertion as to what are the facts, but the very fact that there is some controversy as to whether this is or is not the fairest way to distribute the amount that we are asking parliament to appropriate for the Canadian universities is a reason I had in the back of my mind when making the suggestion that this fund should be turned over to the national conference of Canadian universities.
Of course they will not have any discretion under the contract to depart from the formula that will be set down, but they will have the right-and I feel quite certain they will exercise that right-to make recommendations as to what should be the terms of subsequent votes of this amount, and their suggestions to the government will be brought to the attention of the House of Commons with such recommendations about them as we may feel would be in the best interests of university activities throughout the country.
I am not making any assertion as to what are the facts but I have been told that, although it is true that in Nova Scotia there are quite a number of students enrolled who come from other provinces, the universities they attend are paid quite substantial additional fees because these students come from other provinces. I have been told, with respect to those who come from Newfoundland, that additional fees are provided by the government of Newfoundland or by the institutions in Newfoundland that participate in this grant. They are not able themselves to supply all the forms of university training their people require and there is a transfer of funds by them to the universities of Nova Scotia which perform the job for them.
These institutions, especially in the maritime provinces, are private enterprise institutions, and can fix and adjust their fees according to the localities from which their students come. That is one reason why there may apparently be less paid per capita of student enrolment than there is paid in Newfoundland, for example, where student enrolments in their institutions are much fewer per 100,000 of population than in the case of Nova Scotia. I am told that another reason for the difference is that in Nova Scotia a student who continues beyond the 11th grade is treated as of university level, while in Ontario only students who continue beyond the 13th grade are treated as of university level. That would affect the number of student enrolments.

These are matters about which I know very little, but they are matters which the members of the national conference of Canadian universities can inquire into very pertinently. I discussed with several members of the conference whether it would be appropriate at this time to try to devise some other formula that would not leave discrepancies that look so large, and I was told that many of them believed that this was the fairest formula but that these were matters that could be discussed by their conference.
The people who form this conference are all dedicated men and women. They are devoting their lives to a job they think is in the interests of their fellow citizens, and they can make observations. If as a result of their observations there is another formula that will serve better the desire of the house that the best possible use be made of the money appropriated by parliament to aid universities, their recommendations will be brought to the attention of the house. Every year there will have to be a vote in terms that will in substance be similar to the terms used in the item in the present supplementary estimate. If on their report it appears desirable that there be some change in the formula incorporated in the expressions used for that vote, those changes can be made.
I am sure that all those connected with the matter are sincerely and genuinely concerned that the amounts voted by parliament be used in the best possible way for the necessary aid to the continuance and, I hope, the progressive development of our university institutions. I do not think there is anything else I need to add. I noted the remarks of the hon. member for Three Rivers. He is one of those who fear that from this there would flow some intervention that would lessen in some degree the practical effect of the jurisdiction of the provincial legislature over universities. I am sorry I cannot convince him that he is wrong, but I must tell him that he cannot convince me that I am wrong, and I am submitting the item to the judgment of the house.

Mr. Chairman, it is very reassuring, I am sure, to hear the Prime Minister say there will be no interference with provincial autonomy in the matter of education. I suppose we will have to take his word for it, but I am still at a loss to know what difference there is between this principle as enunciated by the Prime Minister tonight and in a previous speech, and that enunciated by the Minister of Justice yesterday. I have here today's Ottawa Citizen. We know what the Minister of Justice said yesterday, but here in glaring headlines it says: "Federal Grants Would Cost Provinces Their Autonomy

in Education-Garson." Here is the smiling gentleman's picture and under it the words, "Hon. Stuart Garson-Autonomy Would End."
I know the Minister of Justice was speaking in a different debate. I know the subject may have been technically different, but in principle I cannot see how there can be any difference. The resolution under debate yesterday called for assistance to the provinces by way of federal grants, and the principle involved in the present debate is also grants to the provinces. The only difference is in the mechanics by which the money travels, but the principle is the same. I wish the Prime Minister could give us an explanation of that. I should like to ask the Prime Minister a question. What the Prime Minister has been saying in the last few minutes has given me a somewhat different view of the national conference of Canadian universities, which we discussed this afternoon. speechtext: An advisory function.

No more after this item is passed than they have been able to do in the past. They have frequently made recommendations to me as to what might be helpful in the prosecution of university work. I sought advice from several of them as to the possibility of removing this complaint that has been made for the last six years by Nova Scotia authorities, about the fact that their per capita per student grant was smaller than that of the other provinces.
My first answer was this. If you have a larger proportion of students who are getting university training, is that not evidence that

Supply-Health and Welfare in the other provinces where the proportion is smaller the need is even greater as in Nova Scotia? But then gradually I received other assertions-ones that I did not feel I was competent to verify-that the whole story did not appear in this apparent discrepancy between the per student grant in each province.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader

Yes, Mr. Chairman. I will make a brief explanation and give a more detailed one later if it is desirable. Briefly the United Nations, as the committee knows, is now clearing the Suez canal of the obstructions which were placed there during the late fall. That work is estimated to cost somewhere between $30 and $40 million. That is a very

preliminary and tentative estimate, of course As I have said, the work is being done under the direction of the United Nations and the UN has no money for this particular work. Consequently the secretary general of the United Nations asked that he have put in hand the sum of $10 million as soon as possible by those nations which would find it possible to advance that sum in order to pay the cost of the job from day to day and from week to week.
After considering the matter it was decided to recommend to the committee and to the house that we should advance $1 million on a temporary loan basis to the secretary general of the United Nations to help finance the job that has to be done before the canal can be put in use again. The following is the answer to an oral question asked on January 16 by the hon. member for Lambton West, which appeared at page 298 of Hansard.

1.	How did it become possible for the United States supreme court to determine the flow of water through the Chicago drainage canal?
2.	In his veto of the bill for increasing diversion of water from lake Michigan, did President Eisenhower state that he would not permit more water to go through the Chicago drainage canal?
3.	Did the Secretary of State for External Affairs make a statement that the Chicago diversion was a matter for the international joint commission?
4.	Would our supreme court or any judicial body in this country be empowered to permit a similar diversion from lake Huron or lake Erie?
Answer by:	Mr. Cardin, Parliamentary
Assistant, for the Secretary of State for
External Affairs:
1.	This is a matter of United States domestic law and accordingly is outside our competence to answer. However, the following outline of my understanding of the situation may be helpful. A United States statute of 1890 forbids the alteration or modification of the course of any navigable waters of the United States without authorization by the Secretary of War. In 1899 the Secretary of War granted permission to the Chicago sanitary district to divert a certain quantity of water from lake Michigan into the Chicago drainage canal. Litigation concerning this authorization came before the Supreme Court of the United States which issued a formal order on April 21, 1930, limiting the volume of water which might be diverted at Chicago to an annual average of 1,500 cubic feet per second in addition to domestic pumpage of some 1,700 cubic feet per second. The order apparently is of a continuing nature and to obtain authority to divert a greater amount of water, an application must be made to the Supreme Court of the United States to vary its order of 1930. On December 17, 1956, the United States Supreme Court varied its order to increase the flow from 1,500 to 8,500 cubic feet per second (in addition to domestic pumpage) beginning immediately and continuing until January 31, 1957. The representations on the basis of which the court made its order were that, as a result of a serious drought in the American middle west, navigation on the Mississippi river had been seriously affected and that emergency conditions existed.
2.	No. In his memorandum of disapproval dated August 9, 1956, President Eisenhower states that he has withheld his approval of House of Representatives Bill 3210. This bill
Question
proposed to increase the diversion of water from lake Michigan by 1,000 cubic feet per second for a three-year test period. I suppose, as legislation, it would in effect override the court order. In part, the President's memorandum says: "A comprehensive report by the corps of engineers which will include consideration of the best methods of obtaining improved control of the levels of the great lakes and of preventing recurrence of damage along the shores is nearing completion. I am asking the Secretary of Defence to expedite completion of this report. This report is in addition to the technical report on the effects of an increased diversion into the Illinois waterway which has been made by the joint lake Ontario engineering board to the international joint commission. I think it would be unwise to proceed with the diversion in the manner proposed in H.R. 3210 until all relevant information has been obtained, particularly since objections to the proposed diversion have been registered by the Canadian government in its note dated February 13, 1956, and additional objections filed by legal advisers of the states of Wisconsin, Ohio, and New York. ... I am asking the state department to engage in discussions with the Canadian government in an attempt to work out a solution to these problems as soon as all pertinent facts are available." I may add that the Canadian government has not yet been approached by the state department, although recent newspaper reports indicate that such action may be expected soon.
3.	No. On the contrary, on August 2, 1956, in replying to a question from the hon. member for Lambton West, the Secretary of State for External Affairs is quoted in Hansard, at page 6844: "It appears that the proposed diversion of the waters of lake Michigan would not come under the jurisdiction of the international joint commission unless it were referred specifically to it."
4.	No. Lake Huron and lake Erie are boundary waters and article III of the boundary waters treaty provides that no "diversions, whether temporary or permanent, of boundary waters on either side of the line, affecting the natural level or flow of boundary waters on the other side of the line, shall be made except by authority of the United States or the Dominion of Canada within their respective jurisdictions and with the approval, as hereinafter provided, of a joint commission, to be known as the international joint commission." The article goes on to explain that this provision is not intended to limit the right of each government to undertake certain governmental works in boundary waters which "do not

materially affect the level or flow of the boundary waters on the other (side of the line), nor are such provisions intended to interfere with the ordinary use of such waters for domestic and sanitary purposes". A diversion from lake Huron or lake Erie would not be similar to a diversion of water from lake Michigan because the latter is not a boundary water. Diversion of waters from lake Michigan comes under article II of the treaty, in which each government reserves to itself ''the exclusive jurisdiction and control over the use and diversion, whether temporary or permanent, of all waters on its own side of the line, which in their natural channels would flow across the boundary or into boundary waters".
